questions.question: What is the COALESCE function used for?
questions.answer: It evaluates arguments sequentially and returns the first non-NULL value in the list.

questions.question: Name three common SQL Server aggregate functions.
questions.answer: COUNT(), SUM(), and AVG().

topics.title: Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
topics.html:
Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)

Course: SQL Server

Simplify complex queries using nested subqueries, Correlated Subqueries, and Common Table Expressions (CTEs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Subquery: A query nested inside another query (e.g. in the WHERE clause).
  • CTE (WITH): A temporary named result set defined within the execution scope of a single query.
  • Correlated Subquery: A nested query that references columns from the outer query, running once per row.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
WITH Sales_CTE AS (
    SELECT SalesPersonId, SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY SalesPersonId
)
SELECT * FROM Sales_CTE WHERE TotalSales > 50000;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using deeply nested subqueries instead of CTEs, which makes SQL code hard to read and maintain.

questions.question: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?
questions.answer: A temporary named result set that can be referenced within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement.

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
questions.answer: A subquery that depends on columns from the outer query and is executed once for each row processed by the outer query.

topics.title: Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions
topics.html:
Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions

Course: SQL Server

Encapsulate SQL logic into reusable databases assets: Stored Procedures and User Defined Functions (UDFs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Stored Procedure: Precompiled SQL code block. Can return multiple datasets, modify data, and take parameters.
  • User Defined Function (UDF): Calculates and returns a single scalar value or a table. Cannot modify data.
  • Execution Plan Caching: Procedures compile once and cache plans for faster subsequent executions.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE PROCEDURE GetEmployeeById @EmpId INT
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Id = @EmpId;
END;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using scalar User Defined Functions inside SELECT lists on large tables, which causes SQL Server to execute the function row-by-row (RBAR - Row By Agonizing Row) and ruins performance.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a Stored Procedure and a Function?
questions.answer: Procedures can modify database tables and execute transactions. Functions cannot modify state and must return a value.

questions.question: What is parameter sniffing?
questions.answer: A compilation behavior where SQL Server compiles a procedure plan using the parameters passed on the first run, which can be inefficient for other parameter values.

topics.title: Views & Triggers
topics.html:
Views & Triggers

Course: SQL Server

Create virtual tables using Views, and intercept database actions (Insert, Update, Delete) using Triggers.

💡 Key Concepts

  • View: A virtual table based on a SELECT query. Simplifies security and complex queries.
  • DML Triggers: Code executed automatically when data in a table is modified.
  • Inserted & Deleted Tables: Temporary tables accessible inside triggers containing row state modifications.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE VIEW ActiveEmployees AS
SELECT Id, Name FROM Employees WHERE IsActive = 1;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Overusing Triggers to manage business logic, which makes debugging extremely difficult because code runs invisibly.

questions.question: What are the Inserted and Deleted tables in triggers?
questions.answer: Temporary, memory-resident tables containing the state of rows before and after the modification.

questions.question: Does a view store data physically?
questions.answer: No, standard views are virtual tables. Indexed views (materialized views), however, do store data physically on disk.

topics.title: ACID Properties & Transactions
topics.html:
ACID Properties & Transactions

Course: SQL Server

Ensure database integrity using transactions that satisfy ACID properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Atomicity: Ensures all database actions in a transaction succeed, or all roll back (All-or-Nothing).
  • Consistency: Guarantees the database transitions from one valid state to another.
  • Isolation / Durability: Isolation keeps concurrent transactions separate. Durability ensures committed changes survive crashes.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance -= 100 WHERE Id = 1;
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance += 100 WHERE Id = 2;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
END CATCH;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Leaving transactions open by forgetting COMMIT or ROLLBACK, which blocks locks and causes database freezes.

questions.question: What does ACID stand for?
questions.answer: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, the core principles of reliable database transactions.

questions.question: What happens if a SQL query fails inside a BEGIN TRANSACTION block without error handling?
questions.answer: The transaction remains open and lock resources stay blocked until the connection is closed or rolled back.

topics.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
topics.html:
Transaction Isolation Levels

Course: SQL Server

Control database locks behavior and prevent anomalies like Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Read Uncommitted: Allows reading uncommitted data, causing Dirty Reads. Low lock overhead.
  • Read Committed: Default level. Prevents dirty reads by holding shared locks until reads finish.
  • Serializable: Highest isolation. Places range locks to prevent phantom reads.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM Products;
COMMIT TRANSACTION;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Setting isolation level to Serializable unnecessarily, which blocks concurrent queries and slows down execution.

questions.question: What is a dirty read?
questions.answer: Reading data that has been modified by an active transaction but has not yet been committed.

questions.question: How does Snapshot isolation prevent locking readers?
questions.answer: It uses row versioning in tempdb to show readers the data state at the start of the transaction, avoiding shared locks.

topics.title: Indexing Strategies & Query Optimization
topics.html:
Indexing Strategies & Query Optimization

Course: SQL Server

Optimize database tables using Clustered and Non-Clustered indexes, and analyze execution plans.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Clustered Index: Re-orders table data physically on disk. Only 1 per table.
  • Non-Clustered Index: A separate search index pointing to row IDs. Multiple allowed.
  • Covering Index: Adding INCLUDE columns to indexes so queries resolve entirely within the index.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Id ON Employees(Id);
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Email ON Employees(Email) INCLUDE(Name);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adding indexes to every column, which slows down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries because all indexes must be rebuilt.

questions.question: What is a covering index?
questions.answer: An index that contains all the columns referenced by a query, allowing results to resolve without table lookups.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Index Scan and an Index Seek?
questions.answer: A scan searches the entire index tree (slow). A seek navigates directly to matching rows using search keys (fast).

topics.title: Database Normalization
topics.html:
Database Normalization

Course: SQL Server

Minimize data redundancy and prevent anomalies by normalizing tables into 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF.

💡 Key Concepts

  • 1NF (First Normal Form): Atomic columns and unique rows. No repeating groups.
  • 2NF (Second Normal Form): Meets 1NF. Removes partial dependencies (all columns depend on the entire primary key).
  • 3NF (Third Normal Form): Meets 2NF. Removes transitive dependencies (non-key columns depend only on the primary key).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// 3NF Rule: ZipCode table should hold City/State columns,
// and Customers table should only store ZipCodeId.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Over-normalizing simple databases, which requires joining too many tables for basic queries and slows down performance.

questions.question: What is transitive dependency in 3NF?
questions.answer: When a non-key column depends on another non-key column, rather than directly on the primary key.

questions.question: When is denormalization acceptable?
questions.answer: In read-heavy reporting systems (Data Warehouses) to reduce JOIN complexity and speed up reads.

topics.title: SQL Server Security Policies
topics.html:
SQL Server Security Policies

Course: SQL Server

Secure database instances using logins, users, schemas, and Row-Level Security (RLS).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Logins vs Users: Logins grant server connection access. Users grant access to specific databases.
  • Row-Level Security (RLS): Filters query rows automatically based on user roles and security predicates.
  • SQL Injection Prevention: Always use parameterized queries, never concatenate SQL strings.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE SECURITY POLICY SalesFilter
ADD FILTRATION PREDICATE dbo.fn_securitypredicate(SalesPersonId)
ON dbo.Orders;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using the "sa" (system administrator) account for application connections, exposing full database access.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Login and a User?
questions.answer: A Login is for server authentication. A User is database-specific, mapping a login to table access.

questions.question: How do parameterized queries prevent SQL injection?
questions.answer: By treating inputs strictly as literal values rather than executable SQL commands.

topics.title: Disaster Recovery (Backup & Restore)
topics.html:
Disaster Recovery (Backup & Restore)

Course: SQL Server

Plan database recovery strategies using Full, Differential, and Transaction Log backups.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Backup Types: Full (entire DB), Differential (changes since last Full), Log (changes since last Log backup).
  • Recovery Models: Simple (no log backups, auto-truncates), Full (retains transaction logs, allows point-in-time recovery).
  • Point-In-Time Restore: Restoring a database to a specific second before a corruption event.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
BACKUP DATABASE TutorialDb TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\TutorialDb.bak';
BACKUP LOG TutorialDb TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\TutorialDb_Log.trn';

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Running database recovery in Full Recovery Model without setting up Transaction Log backups, causing transaction log files (.ldf) to grow until the disk is full.

questions.question: Why does the transaction log grow continuously in Full Recovery Model?
questions.answer: Because SQL Server keeps the log until a Transaction Log backup is run to truncate committed logs.

questions.question: What is a differential backup?
questions.answer: A backup that contains all changes made to the database since the last full database backup.

topics.title: React
topics.html:
Section 1: React Fundamentals

1. Tell me about React.

  • React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces developed by Meta.
  • It follows a component-based architecture, allowing developers to create reusable UI components and compose them into complex applications.
  • One of React's key strengths is its Virtual DOM, which improves performance by updating only the parts of the UI that have changed.
  • React is commonly used for building Single Page Applications (SPAs) where maintainability, reusability, and performance are important.
  • It is often combined with APIs, Context API, Redux Toolkit, and React Router.

Real Project Example

In my project, I created reusable components such as DataTable, SearchBar, Pagination, and Modal. These components were reused across multiple screens, reducing duplicate code and making maintenance easier.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why choose React over Angular?
React gives more flexibility because it's a library rather than a complete framework. We can choose our own routing, state management, and architecture based on project needs.
Q: Why choose React over Vanilla JavaScript?
React provides component reusability, state management, efficient rendering, and a structured way to build large applications.

2. What is JSX?

  • JSX stands for JavaScript XML.
  • It allows developers to write HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript code.
  • Browsers do not understand JSX directly.
  • During the build process, Babel converts JSX into React.createElement() calls.
  • JSX improves readability and developer productivity by keeping UI structure and logic together.

💻 Practical Code Example 

const element = <h1>Hello React</h1>;

⚙️ Internally Converted To 

React.createElement(
  "h1",
  null,
  "Hello React"
);

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use className instead of class?
Because class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript, React uses className instead.

3. What is the Virtual DOM?

  • The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the actual DOM.
  • Whenever state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree.
  • React compares the new tree with the previous tree.
  • Only the changed elements are updated in the real DOM.
  • This significantly improves performance because DOM operations are expensive.

Real Example

  • Imagine a page displaying 100 products.
  • Without React, a large portion of the UI may re-render.
  • With React, only the changed product gets updated.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Does React directly update the DOM?
No. React first updates the Virtual DOM and then updates only the necessary parts of the real DOM.

4. What is Reconciliation?

  • Reconciliation is React's algorithm for comparing the previous Virtual DOM tree with the new Virtual DOM tree.
  • Its purpose is to determine the minimum number of changes required in the real DOM.
  • This process is commonly known as Diffing.

Interview Shortcut

  • Virtual DOM creates snapshots.
  • Reconciliation compares snapshots.
  • React updates only what is different.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between Virtual DOM and Reconciliation?
Virtual DOM is the data structure. Reconciliation is the process used to compare Virtual DOM trees and determine updates.

5. What are Components in React?

  • Components are reusable building blocks of a React application.
  • Each component contains its own UI and logic.
  • Breaking applications into components improves maintainability, reusability, and testability.

📂 Example Structure 

App
├ Navbar
├ Sidebar
├ ProductList
└ Footer

Real Project Example

Instead of creating separate tables everywhere, I usually build a reusable DataTable component and pass configuration through props.

6. Functional Components vs Class Components

  • Functional components are JavaScript functions that return JSX.
  • Class components are ES6 classes that extend React.Component.
  • Modern React development prefers functional components because Hooks provide state management and lifecycle capabilities.

💻 Functional Component 

function User() {
  return <h1>User</h1>;
}

💻 Class Component 

class User extends React.Component {
  render() {
    return <h1>User</h1>;
  }
}

Which One Do You Use?

In modern React development, functional components are preferred because they are simpler, cleaner, and fully support Hooks.

7. What are Props?

  • Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child component.
  • They make components reusable and configurable.
  • Props are read-only and should never be modified by child components.

💻 Example 

<User name="Ashutosh" />
function User(props) {
  return <h1>{props.name}</h1>;
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Can props be modified?
No. Props are immutable. If data needs to change, state should be used.

8. What is State?

  • State represents data managed within a component.
  • Unlike props, state can change over time.
  • Whenever state changes, React automatically re-renders the component.

💻 Example 

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Props vs State

Props State
Passed from parent Managed internally
Read-only Can change
External data Internal data

9. Why Should State Not Be Updated Directly?

❌ Bad Example

count = count + 1;

✅ Correct Example

setCount(count + 1);
  • React tracks updates through state setter functions.
  • Directly modifying state bypasses React's rendering system.
  • This can cause UI inconsistencies and unexpected behavior.
Q: Why does React need setState/useState setters?
React uses these functions to schedule updates and trigger re-renders efficiently.

10. What are Keys in React?

  • Keys help React uniquely identify elements inside lists.
  • During reconciliation, React uses keys to determine which elements were added, removed, or updated.
  • Proper keys improve rendering accuracy and performance.

💻 Example 

users.map(user => (
  <User
    key={user.id}
    user={user}
  />
))

Common Mistake

key={index}
Q: Why avoid using index as a key?
If list order changes, React may incorrectly reuse components, causing rendering bugs and performance issues.

Section 2: Hooks Deep Dive

11. What is useState?

  • useState is a React Hook that allows functional components to manage state.
  • Before Hooks were introduced, state management was only possible in class components.
  • useState made it possible to manage state directly inside functional components.
  • It returns an array containing the current state value and a function to update that state.

💻 Example

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Real Project Example

In a search screen, I use useState to manage search text, loading states, selected filters, and API results.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Does updating state immediately update the value?
No. State updates are asynchronous. React schedules the update and re-renders the component.
Q: How do you update state based on previous state? 
setCount(prev => prev + 1);
This avoids stale state issues.

12. What is useEffect?

  • useEffect is used to handle side effects in React components.
  • Side effects include API calls, subscriptions, timers, event listeners, logging, or any operation outside React's rendering process.
  • It allows developers to perform actions after a component renders.

💻 Example

useEffect(() => {
  fetchUsers();
}, []);

Real Project Example

Whenever a page loads, I use useEffect to call backend APIs and populate the UI.

Follow-up Questions

Q: When does useEffect run?
By default, after every render unless controlled by dependencies.
Q: Can we make API calls inside useEffect?
Yes. API calls are one of the most common use cases for useEffect.

13. Dependency Array in useEffect

  • The dependency array controls when useEffect executes.
  • Incorrect dependencies are one of the most common causes of React bugs.

Case 1: No Dependency Array

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Runs every render");
});
Runs after every render.

Case 2: Empty Dependency Array

useEffect(() => {
  fetchData();
}, []);
Runs only once when the component mounts.

Case 3: With Dependencies

useEffect(() => {
  searchUsers();
}, [searchTerm]);
Runs whenever searchTerm changes.

Interview Tip

Understanding dependency arrays is critical because most React bugs involving useEffect come from incorrect dependencies.

14. What is the Cleanup Function?

  • Cleanup functions prevent memory leaks.
  • They remove resources when a component unmounts or before the effect runs again.
  • Cleanup is commonly used for subscriptions, timers, and event listeners.

💻 Example

useEffect(() => {
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    console.log("Running");
  }, 1000);

  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, []);

Real Project Example

When listening for browser resize events, I remove the listener during cleanup to prevent memory leaks.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is cleanup important?
Without cleanup, subscriptions, timers, and event listeners remain active even after a component is removed.

15. What Causes Infinite Loops in useEffect?

  • Infinite loops happen when an effect updates state that is also listed as a dependency.
  • The effect continuously triggers itself through state updates.
  • This results in repeated re-renders and performance issues.

💻 Example

useEffect(() => {
  setCount(count + 1);
}, [count]);

What Happens?

count changes
↓
effect runs
↓
state updates
↓
re-render
↓
effect runs again

Solution

Review dependencies carefully and avoid unnecessary state updates inside effects.

Interview Tip

Infinite loop questions are extremely common in React interviews.

16. What is useRef?

  • useRef provides a mutable object whose value persists across renders.
  • Updating a ref does not trigger a component re-render.
  • It is commonly used for DOM access and storing mutable values.
  • The current value is available through the .current property.

💻 Example

const inputRef = useRef();

💻 Accessing DOM Elements

inputRef.current.focus();

Real Project Example

After opening a modal, I automatically focus the first input field using useRef to improve user experience.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Does updating useRef trigger re-render?
No. React does not track changes to the current property for rendering purposes.
Q: Difference between useRef and useState?
useState triggers re-renders when updated, while useRef stores values without causing re-renders.

17. What is useMemo?

  • useMemo is a performance optimization Hook that memoizes expensive calculations.
  • It prevents recalculating values when dependencies have not changed.
  • It should be used only when the calculation cost is significant.
  • useMemo returns a cached value.

💻 Example

const total = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateTotal(products);
}, [products]);

Real Project Example

In reporting dashboards, I use useMemo to calculate totals, aggregations, and filtered datasets efficiently.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Should useMemo be used everywhere?
No. useMemo itself has overhead. Use it only for expensive computations.
Q: Is useMemo guaranteed optimization?
No. It is a performance hint, not a guarantee. React may still recompute values when needed.

18. What is useCallback?

  • useCallback memoizes functions so React doesn't create a new function instance on every render.
  • It helps prevent unnecessary re-renders when passing callbacks to child components.
  • useCallback returns a memoized function reference.

💻 Example

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  console.log("clicked");
}, []);

Real Project Example

When passing event handlers to child components wrapped with React.memo, I use useCallback to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why not just define functions normally?
A new function gets created on every render. This can cause child components to re-render unnecessarily when function identity changes.

19. useMemo vs useCallback

  • Both are optimization Hooks.
  • useMemo memoizes computed values.
  • useCallback memoizes functions.
  • Both rely on dependency arrays.

useMemo

const total = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateTotal(items);
}, [items]);
Returns a cached value.

useCallback

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  console.log("clicked");
}, []);
Returns a cached function reference.

Interview Shortcut

  • useMemo caches results.
  • useCallback caches functions.

20. What is useReducer?

  • useReducer is a Hook used for complex state management.
  • State transitions are handled through actions and reducers.
  • It provides better structure when state logic becomes complicated.
  • It is commonly used as an alternative to multiple useState calls.

💻 Example

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(
  reducer,
  initialState
);

Why Use It?

Add User
Delete User
Update User
Reset User
Managing these actions with multiple useState calls can become difficult. useReducer centralizes state transition logic into a single reducer function.

Real Project Example

I use useReducer for large forms with multiple fields, validation rules, and complex state transitions.

Interview Tip

When state transitions resemble business actions, useReducer often provides a cleaner and more maintainable solution than multiple useState calls.

21. When Would You Choose useReducer Over useState?

  • useState works best for simple and independent pieces of state.
  • useReducer is better when state transitions become complex.
  • It provides a centralized way to handle state updates.
  • Complex business workflows are often easier to manage with reducers.

Good Candidates for useState

Counter
Input Field
Modal Open/Close
Loading State

Good Candidates for useReducer

Large Forms
Complex Validation
Business Workflows
Multiple Related States

Interview Shortcut

useState is simpler. useReducer provides better structure for complex state transitions.

22. What is useContext?

  • useContext allows components to consume values from React Context.
  • It eliminates the need to manually pass props through multiple levels.
  • It helps solve the problem of prop drilling.
  • Any component inside a Context Provider can access shared data directly.

Problem Without Context

App
 ↓
Parent
 ↓
Child
 ↓
GrandChild
User information must be passed through every component level.

With Context API

Context Provider
 ↓
Any Component
Components can directly access shared values without intermediate props.

Real Project Example

I use Context for authenticated user information, application themes, language settings, and permissions.

23. What are Custom Hooks?

  • Custom Hooks are reusable JavaScript functions that internally use React Hooks.
  • They allow stateful logic to be shared across multiple components.
  • They improve code reuse and maintainability.
  • Custom Hooks typically start with the word "use".

💻 Example

function useUsers() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchUsers();
  }, []);

  return users;
}

Real Project Example

Instead of repeating API-fetching logic across multiple screens, I create reusable hooks such as useUsers(), useProducts(), and useAuth().

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Custom Hooks?
Custom Hooks improve code reuse, reduce duplication, and make components easier to maintain.

24. What is useLayoutEffect?

  • useLayoutEffect is similar to useEffect but runs synchronously before the browser paints the screen.
  • It is mainly used for DOM measurements and layout calculations.
  • It can help prevent visual flickering.
  • Most applications only need useEffect.

Execution Order

Render
↓
useLayoutEffect
↓
Paint

useEffect Order

Render
↓
Paint
↓
useEffect

Real Project Example

When calculating element dimensions before rendering, I use useLayoutEffect to avoid layout shifts and flickering.

Interview Tip

If you are unsure which one to use, choose useEffect. useLayoutEffect is intended for special DOM-related scenarios.

25. What is forwardRef?

  • forwardRef allows parent components to access a child component's DOM element.
  • It forwards a ref through a component to one of its child elements.
  • It is commonly used when building reusable form and UI components.

💻 Example

const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => {
  return <input ref={ref} />;
});

Parent Component

const inputRef = useRef();

Real Project Example

I use forwardRef in reusable form components where parent components need access to focus, validation, or scrolling functionality.

Common Use Cases

  • Auto Focus Inputs
  • Reusable Form Components
  • React Hook Form Integration
  • Custom UI Libraries

26. What is useImperativeHandle?

  • useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent component can access through a ref.
  • It is commonly used together with forwardRef.
  • Instead of exposing an entire component, it exposes only selected methods.
  • This improves encapsulation and creates cleaner component APIs.

💻 Example

useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  focusInput() {
    inputRef.current.focus();
  }
}));

Why Use It?

Instead of exposing the entire child component, expose only specific methods that the parent needs.

Real Project Example

I use useImperativeHandle in reusable modal and form components where parent components need controlled access to open, close, reset, or focus functionality.

27. What are the Rules of Hooks?

  • React Hooks follow strict rules to ensure consistent execution order.
  • Breaking these rules can cause React to associate state with the wrong Hook.
  • These rules exist because React tracks Hooks by position, not by name.

Rule 1: Only Call Hooks at the Top Level

❌ Wrong

if (loggedIn) {
  useEffect(() => {});
}
✅ Correct

useEffect(() => {
  if (loggedIn) {
    // logic
  }
}, [loggedIn]);

Rule 2: Only Call Hooks From

  • Functional Components
  • Custom Hooks
❌ Wrong

function fetchUsers() {
  useState();
}

Why?

React relies on a consistent Hook execution order across renders.

Interview One-Liner

Hooks must always execute in the same order on every render.

28. Explain useEffect Lifecycle

  • useEffect can simulate lifecycle methods from class components.
  • It can handle component mounting, updating, and unmounting.
  • Its behavior depends on the dependency array.

Mount Phase

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Mounted");
}, []);
Runs once when the component loads. Equivalent to componentDidMount().

Update Phase

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Search changed");
}, [searchTerm]);
Runs whenever searchTerm changes. Equivalent to componentDidUpdate().

Unmount Phase

useEffect(() => {
  return () => {
    console.log("Cleanup");
  };
}, []);
Runs when the component is removed. Equivalent to componentWillUnmount().

Real Project Example

On a User Management page, I use useEffect to load users during mount, refresh data when filters change, and remove subscriptions during unmount.

Follow-up Question

Q: Can useEffect replace all lifecycle methods?
Almost all common lifecycle functionality can be handled using useEffect.

29. Difference Between useEffect and useLayoutEffect

  • Both Hooks execute side effects.
  • The main difference is when they run.
  • useLayoutEffect runs before the browser paints.
  • useEffect runs after the browser paints.

useEffect Execution Flow

Render
 ↓
Browser Paint
 ↓
useEffect

useLayoutEffect Execution Flow

Render
 ↓
useLayoutEffect
 ↓
Browser Paint

Practical Example

useLayoutEffect(() => {
  console.log(divRef.current.offsetWidth);
}, []);
When measuring element dimensions before rendering, useLayoutEffect prevents visual flickering.

Real Project Example

Most business applications only require useEffect. I use useLayoutEffect only when DOM measurements must occur before the user sees the page.

Interview Tip

If you're unsure, use useEffect. useLayoutEffect is intended for specialized DOM-related scenarios.

30. What Causes Infinite Loops in useEffect?

  • Infinite loops occur when an effect continuously updates one of its own dependencies.
  • The update triggers a re-render, which runs the effect again.
  • This process repeats indefinitely.

Example

useEffect(() => {
  setCount(count + 1);
}, [count]);

Execution Flow

count changes
↓
effect runs
↓
setCount
↓
re-render
↓
effect runs again

Common Causes

  • Updating state inside an effect that depends on that state.
  • Using recreated functions as dependencies.
  • Using recreated objects or arrays as dependencies.

Problematic Function Dependency

const fetchData = () => {};

useEffect(() => {
  fetchData();
}, [fetchData]);

Solution

const fetchData = useCallback(() => {
}, []);

Interview Tip

Most useEffect bugs are caused by incorrect dependencies, recreated functions, or recreated objects.

31. useRef vs useState

  • Both Hooks can store values between renders.
  • useState triggers component re-renders when updated.
  • useRef does not trigger re-renders.
  • Choosing the wrong Hook can impact performance and behavior.

Comparison Table

Feature useState useRef
Triggers Re-render Yes No
Stores Values Yes Yes
DOM Access No Yes
UI Updates Yes No

Example

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

const renderCount = useRef(0);

renderCount.current++;
Updating count re-renders the component. Updating renderCount.current does not.

Interview Tip

Use useState when the UI must update. Use useRef when you need to store values without causing re-renders.

32. Advanced useMemo vs useCallback

  • Both Hooks are performance optimization tools.
  • useMemo caches calculated values.
  • useCallback caches function references.
  • Overusing either Hook can reduce readability and sometimes hurt performance.

useMemo Example

const filteredUsers = useMemo(() => {
  return users.filter(user =>
    user.active
  );
}, [users]);
The expensive filtering operation runs only when users changes.

useCallback Example

const handleDelete = useCallback(
  (id) => {
    deleteUser(id);
  },
  []
);
The function reference remains stable between renders.

Common Mistake

  • Using useMemo for every variable.
  • Using useCallback for every function.
  • Optimizing before identifying performance bottlenecks.

Interview One-Liner

useMemo caches values. useCallback caches functions.

33. When Should You Use useReducer?

  • useReducer is ideal when state transitions become complex.
  • It centralizes update logic into a reducer function.
  • It improves maintainability when multiple actions affect the same state.
  • It follows a predictable action-driven update pattern.

Poor Fit for useState

Add Product
Delete Product
Update Product
Reset Product
Validate Product
Managing these actions using multiple useState calls quickly becomes difficult.

Better with useReducer

dispatch({
  type: "ADD_PRODUCT",
  payload: product
});
Reducers centralize all business logic in a single location.

Real Project Example

I often use useReducer in complex forms, shopping carts, workflow engines, and multi-step wizards.

34. Context API vs Redux

  • Both Context API and Redux help manage shared application state.
  • Context API is built into React.
  • Redux is a dedicated state management library.
  • Redux provides advanced debugging and middleware capabilities.

Comparison Table

Feature Context API Redux Toolkit
Built Into React Yes No
DevTools Limited Excellent
Middleware No Yes
Large Applications Moderate Excellent

When I Use Context API

  • Theme Management
  • User Authentication
  • Language Selection
  • Application Settings

When I Use Redux Toolkit

  • Complex Business Workflows
  • Large Shared State
  • Cross-Module Communication
  • Enterprise Applications

Interview Tip

Context API is not a direct replacement for Redux. They solve different levels of state management complexity.

35. What Are the Advantages of Custom Hooks?

  • Custom Hooks allow reusable stateful logic.
  • They reduce code duplication.
  • They improve maintainability and testability.
  • They help keep components focused on rendering.

Without Custom Hooks

UserPage
  API Logic

AdminPage
  Same API Logic

Dashboard
  Same API Logic
The same logic gets duplicated across multiple components.

With Custom Hooks

useUsers()

UserPage
AdminPage
Dashboard
All components reuse the same Hook.

Real Project Example

I commonly create hooks such as useAuth, useUsers, useProducts, usePagination, and useApi for shared application functionality.

Interview One-Liner

Custom Hooks are a mechanism for sharing stateful logic, not state itself.

36. Why Does useEffect Run Twice in React StrictMode?

  • In React StrictMode (development only), React intentionally runs effects twice.
  • This helps detect side effects that are not properly cleaned up.
  • The double execution does not occur in production builds.
  • It is a debugging feature designed to identify unsafe code.

Example

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("API Called");
}, []);
In development mode with StrictMode enabled, you may see the log appear twice.

Why React Does This

  • Detect missing cleanup logic.
  • Find unexpected side effects.
  • Prepare applications for future React optimizations.

Interview Tip

If useEffect runs twice only in development and not in production, React StrictMode is usually the reason.

37. How Does React Determine Hook Execution Order?

  • React tracks Hooks based on the order in which they are called.
  • React does not identify Hooks by variable names.
  • Hook position must remain consistent across renders.
  • Changing Hook order can cause state corruption.

Example

function User() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [age, setAge] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
  }, []);

  return null;
}
React remembers Hook state by call order: 1st Hook → name 2nd Hook → age 3rd Hook → effect

Why This Matters

If a Hook is skipped or moved, React associates state with the wrong Hook, causing unexpected behavior.

Interview One-Liner

React identifies Hooks by execution order, not by variable names.

38. Why Shouldn't Hooks Be Called Conditionally?

  • Conditional Hook calls change Hook execution order.
  • React expects Hooks to execute in the same sequence every render.
  • Violating this rule can break state management.
  • This is one of the most frequently asked React interview questions.

Incorrect Example

if (loggedIn) {
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchUsers();
  }, []);
}

Correct Example

useEffect(() => {
  if (loggedIn) {
    fetchUsers();
  }
}, [loggedIn]);

What Goes Wrong?

If loggedIn changes, the Hook order changes. React can no longer correctly map state to Hooks.

Interview Tip

Hooks should always be declared at the top level of a component.

39. How Does React Store Hook State Internally?

  • React internally maintains a list of Hook objects for each component.
  • Each Hook call occupies a position in that list.
  • During re-renders, React traverses the list in the same order.
  • This is why Hook order must remain consistent.

Conceptual View

Hook #1 → useState(name)
Hook #2 → useState(age)
Hook #3 → useEffect()
React retrieves Hook state by position rather than by variable names.

Why Interviewers Ask This

This question tests whether a developer understands why the Rules of Hooks exist.

Senior-Level Answer

React maintains Hook state using an internal linked structure associated with each component fiber. Hook order must remain stable for React to correctly associate state with Hook calls.

40. When Can useMemo Hurt Performance?

  • useMemo itself has overhead.
  • React must store cached values and track dependencies.
  • If the calculation is inexpensive, memoization may cost more than recalculation.
  • Premature optimization can reduce code readability.

Bad Example

const fullName = useMemo(() => {
  return firstName + " " + lastName;
}, [firstName, lastName]);
String concatenation is extremely cheap. useMemo adds unnecessary complexity.

Good Example

const report = useMemo(() => {
  return generateLargeReport(data);
}, [data]);
Expensive calculations benefit from memoization.

Common Mistakes

  • Wrapping every variable with useMemo.
  • Using useMemo without performance measurements.
  • Optimizing code that is already fast.

Interview One-Liner

useMemo should be used for expensive computations, not simple calculations.

41. When Can useCallback Hurt Performance?

  • useCallback is not free. React must store the cached function and track dependencies.
  • If a function is simple and not passed to memoized child components, useCallback may provide no benefit.
  • Overusing useCallback can make code harder to read and maintain.
  • Performance optimization should be based on measurement, not assumptions.

Bad Example

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  console.log("Clicked");
}, []);
This function is simple and may not require memoization.

Good Example

const handleDelete = useCallback(
  (id) => {
    deleteUser(id);
  },
  []
);
Useful when passing callbacks to React.memo components.

Interview Tip

Don't use useCallback everywhere. Use it when function identity actually matters.

42. How Would You Debug an Infinite useEffect Loop?

  • First inspect the dependency array.
  • Look for state updates that affect dependencies.
  • Check whether functions, objects, or arrays are recreated on every render.
  • Use React DevTools and browser debugging tools to identify repeated renders.

Common Problem

useEffect(() => {
  setCount(count + 1);
}, [count]);
The effect updates count, which triggers the effect again.

Another Common Problem

const fetchData = () => {};

useEffect(() => {
  fetchData();
}, [fetchData]);
fetchData is recreated during every render.

Possible Fix

const fetchData = useCallback(() => {
}, []);

Debugging Checklist

  • Inspect dependencies.
  • Check state updates inside effects.
  • Check recreated functions.
  • Check recreated objects and arrays.
  • Use React DevTools Profiler.

43. When Should Context API Be Avoided?

  • Context API is excellent for lightweight shared state.
  • However, excessive Context usage can cause unnecessary re-renders.
  • Large applications often benefit from dedicated state management solutions.
  • Not every shared value belongs in Context.

Good Use Cases

  • Theme Management
  • User Authentication
  • Language Selection
  • Application Settings

Poor Use Cases

  • Massive Enterprise State
  • High-Frequency Updates
  • Complex Business Workflows
  • Large Shared Data Graphs

Alternative Solutions

  • Redux Toolkit
  • Zustand
  • Jotai
  • Recoil

Interview One-Liner

Context API solves prop drilling, not all state management problems.

44. Why Doesn't useRef Trigger Re-renders?

  • React only re-renders when state or props change.
  • useRef stores mutable values outside React's rendering workflow.
  • Updating ref.current does not notify React.
  • This behavior makes useRef useful for performance-sensitive scenarios.

Example

const counterRef = useRef(0);

counterRef.current++;
The value changes, but the UI does not automatically re-render.

Compare With State

const [count, setCount] =
  useState(0);

setCount(count + 1);
Updating state triggers React's rendering process.

Interview Tip

useRef is designed for storing mutable values without causing re-renders.

45. What Happens When State Updates Are Batched?

  • React groups multiple state updates together into a single render.
  • This process is known as batching.
  • Batching improves performance by reducing unnecessary renders.
  • React 18 introduced automatic batching in more scenarios.

Example

setName("John");
setAge(30);
setActive(true);
React typically performs a single re-render instead of three separate renders.

Benefits

  • Better Performance
  • Fewer Re-renders
  • Smoother User Experience
  • Reduced DOM Updates

Interview One-Liner

Batching combines multiple state updates into a single render cycle.

46. Explain React.memo and When to Use It

  • React.memo is a higher-order component used to prevent unnecessary re-renders.
  • It memoizes component output based on props.
  • If props do not change, React skips rendering the component.
  • It is useful for expensive child components.

Example

const UserCard = React.memo(
  function UserCard(props) {
    return <div>{props.name}</div>;
  }
);

When It Helps

  • Large Lists
  • Complex Components
  • Dashboard Widgets
  • Expensive UI Rendering

When It Doesn't Help

  • Small Components
  • Components That Always Receive New Props
  • Premature Optimization

Interview Tip

React.memo works best when combined with stable props, useMemo, and useCallback.

47. How Would You Optimize a Slow React Application?

  • Start by measuring performance using React DevTools Profiler.
  • Identify unnecessary re-renders.
  • Optimize expensive computations.
  • Reduce network and rendering overhead.

Optimization Checklist

  • Use React.memo for expensive components.
  • Use useMemo for expensive calculations.
  • Use useCallback for stable function references.
  • Implement code splitting with React.lazy.
  • Virtualize large lists.
  • Optimize API requests.
  • Avoid unnecessary state updates.
  • Use proper keys in lists.

Code Splitting Example

const Dashboard = React.lazy(
  () => import("./Dashboard")
);

Virtualization Example

For thousands of rows, use libraries such as react-window or react-virtualized so only visible items are rendered.

Senior-Level Interview Answer

I first profile the application to identify bottlenecks. Then I target unnecessary re-renders, expensive calculations, large bundle sizes, and inefficient API calls. Optimization should always be data-driven rather than based on assumptions.

Interview One-Liner

Measure first, optimize second.

topics.title: C# Fundamental
topics.html:
Section 1: C# Fundamentals

1. Tell me about C#.

  • C# is a modern, object-oriented, strongly typed programming language developed by Microsoft.
  • It runs on the .NET platform and is widely used for developing web applications, APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, and microservices.
  • One of the key strengths of C# is its support for Object-Oriented Programming, type safety, automatic memory management through Garbage Collection, asynchronous programming with async/await, and a rich class library.
  • In enterprise applications, C# is commonly used with ASP.NET Core for building scalable backend services and REST APIs.

Real Project Example

In one of my projects, I used C# and ASP.NET Core to develop a reporting module that processed large amounts of data from SQL Server. I implemented asynchronous programming using async/await to improve responsiveness and Entity Framework Core for database access. The service exposed REST APIs consumed by a React frontend application.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is C# called a strongly typed language?
C# is strongly typed because every variable and object has a defined data type, and the compiler performs type checking during compilation.

💻 Example

int age = 25;
string name = "Ashutosh";
This helps catch errors early and improves code reliability.
Q: Is C# compiled or interpreted?
C# is compiled into Intermediate Language (IL). At runtime, the CLR uses the JIT compiler to convert IL into native machine code.
Q: What are the main features of C#?
  • Object-Oriented Programming
  • Strong Typing
  • Garbage Collection
  • Exception Handling
  • Generics
  • LINQ
  • Async/Await
  • Delegates and Events
  • Cross-Platform Support through .NET
Q: What is CLR?
CLR (Common Language Runtime) is the execution engine of .NET responsible for memory management, garbage collection, exception handling, security, JIT compilation, and thread management.
  • Memory Management
  • Garbage Collection
  • Exception Handling
  • Security
  • JIT Compilation
  • Thread Management
Q: What is CTS?
CTS (Common Type System) defines how data types are declared and used across all .NET languages, ensuring interoperability.

💻 Example

A class library written in C#
can be used in VB.NET because
both languages follow CTS.
Q: What is CLS?
CLS (Common Language Specification) is a set of rules that .NET languages follow to ensure compatibility with each other.
Q: What is JIT Compiler?
The Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler converts Intermediate Language (IL) code into native machine code at runtime before execution.
Q: What is the difference between .NET and C#?
C# is the programming language, while .NET is the development platform and runtime used to execute C# applications.

💻 Example

C#   → Programming Language

.NET → Development Platform
       and Runtime

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Explain the execution flow of a C# application.
The C# execution process involves compilation into Intermediate Language (IL), loading by the CLR, JIT compilation, and execution as native machine code. 
C# Code
   ↓
Compiler
   ↓
IL Code
   ↓
CLR
   ↓
JIT Compiler
   ↓
Machine Code
   ↓
Execution
  • C# source code is written.
  • The compiler converts it into Intermediate Language (IL).
  • The IL is stored in an assembly (.dll or .exe).
  • CLR loads the assembly.
  • JIT converts IL into native machine code.
  • The operating system executes the machine code.

2. Value Type vs Reference Type

  • In C#, data types are categorized as Value Types and Reference Types.
  • Value Types store the actual value directly.
  • Reference Types store a reference that points to an object in memory.
  • This distinction affects memory allocation, performance, copying behavior, and parameter passing.

Real Project Example

Suppose we have a User model. Understanding Reference Type behavior is critical because multiple variables can point to the same object instance.

💻 Reference Type Example

public class User
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

User user1 = new User();
user1.Name = "Ashutosh";

User user2 = user1;

user2.Name = "John";

Console.WriteLine(user1.Name);
Output: John Both variables reference the same object in memory.

💻 Value Type Example

int number1 = 10;

int number2 = number1;

number2 = 20;

Console.WriteLine(number1);
Output: 10 A separate copy of the value is created.

Memory Representation

Value Type

Stack

number1 = 10
number2 = 20
Each variable stores its own value independently.

Reference Type

Stack

user1 ─────┐
           │
user2 ─────┘

Heap
-------------
Name = John
-------------
Both variables point to the same object stored on the heap.

Common Value Types

int
long
double
decimal
bool
char
DateTime
struct
enum
int age = 30;
decimal salary = 50000;
bool isActive = true;

Common Reference Types

class
string
object
array
delegate
interface
dynamic
string name = "Ashutosh";

int[] numbers = {1,2,3};

User user = new User();

Important Interview Point

String is a Reference Type
Many developers get confused because strings behave similarly to Value Types due to immutability. However, String is actually a class and therefore a Reference Type. 
string name = "Ashutosh";

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the main difference between Value Type and Reference Type?
Value Types store actual values directly, while Reference Types store references to objects.
Q: Give examples of Value Types. 
int
decimal
double
bool
DateTime
struct
enum
Q: Give examples of Reference Types. 
class
string
object
array
delegate
interface
Q: Where are Value Types stored?
Typically on the stack. However, if a Value Type is a member of a Reference Type object, it is stored inside that object on the heap. 
public class Employee
{
    public int Age { get; set; }
}
Q: Where are Reference Types stored?
The object itself is stored on the heap, while the reference variable is usually stored on the stack.
Q: What happens when you assign one Value Type variable to another?
A copy of the value is created, so changes do not affect the original variable. 
int a = 10;
int b = a;

b = 20;
Q: What happens when you assign one Reference Type variable to another?
Only the reference is copied. Both variables point to the same object. 
User user1 = new User();

User user2 = user1;
Q: Why are Value Types generally faster?
They often avoid heap allocation and reduce Garbage Collection overhead, resulting in better performance for small data structures.
Q: What is a Struct?
A Struct is a user-defined Value Type commonly used for small, lightweight objects. 
public struct Point
{
    public int X;
    public int Y;
}
Q: When would you choose Struct over Class?
  • Object is small
  • Object is immutable
  • No inheritance is required
  • High-performance scenarios
Point
DateTime
Guid

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is the impact of Value Types and Reference Types on method parameter passing?
By default, C# passes parameters by value. For Value Types, a copy of the value is passed. For Reference Types, a copy of the reference is passed, but both references still point to the same object.

💻 Value Type Parameter Example

void Update(int x)
{
    x = 100;
}

💻 Reference Type Parameter Example

void Update(User user)
{
    user.Name = "John";
}
The original object can be modified because both references point to the same object instance.

Section 2: Memory Management & Performance

3. Stack vs Heap

  • Stack and Heap are two memory areas used by .NET during program execution.
  • The Stack stores local variables, method parameters, and many Value Types.
  • The Heap stores Reference Type objects and dynamically allocated memory.
  • Understanding Stack and Heap is essential for memory management, object lifetime, and performance optimization.

Real Project Example

Consider a User object and a local integer variable. The integer is stored directly, while the User object is allocated on the Heap and referenced from the Stack.

💻 Example

public class User
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

int age = 30;

User user = new User();

Memory Allocation

Stack
-----
age = 30

user ----->

Heap
-----
User Object
Name = null
The variable age stores its value directly on the stack. The variable user stores a reference on the stack, while the actual User object resides on the heap.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which memory is faster, Stack or Heap?
Stack memory is faster because allocation and deallocation occur automatically in a sequential manner using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) mechanism.
Q: Why is Heap slower?
Heap memory requires dynamic allocation and is managed by the Garbage Collector, which introduces additional overhead.
Q: Does every Value Type always live on the Stack?
No. If a Value Type is a member of a Reference Type object, it becomes part of the object stored on the Heap.
Q: Who manages Stack memory?
The CLR automatically manages stack memory. When a method completes, its stack frame is removed automatically.
Q: Who manages Heap memory?
Heap memory is managed by the Garbage Collector (GC), which automatically reclaims unused objects.

Interview Tip

  • Stack = Fast, Automatic Memory Management
  • Heap = Dynamic Allocation, Garbage Collection
  • Reference Types usually live on Heap
  • Value Types usually live on Stack

4. Boxing vs Unboxing

  • Boxing converts a Value Type into a Reference Type (object).
  • Unboxing converts the boxed object back to its original Value Type.
  • Boxing creates an object on the Heap.
  • Frequent boxing and unboxing can negatively impact performance.

Real Project Example

Boxing commonly occurs when Value Types are stored in collections designed to hold objects. This introduces unnecessary Heap allocations and Garbage Collection overhead.

Boxing

int number = 100;

object obj = number;

Memory Representation

Stack
------
number = 100

obj ----->

Heap
------
100
The integer value is copied into a new object allocated on the Heap.

Unboxing

object obj = 100;

int number = (int)obj;
The object is converted back into its original integer value.

Execution Flow

Value Type
    ↓
 Boxing
    ↓
Object on Heap
    ↓
Unboxing
    ↓
Value Type

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is Boxing expensive?
  • Allocates memory on the Heap
  • Copies the Value Type
  • Increases Garbage Collection workload
  • Consumes additional CPU and memory resources
Q: Why is Unboxing expensive?
  • Requires runtime type checking
  • Copies the value back from the object
  • Adds execution overhead
Q: How can we avoid Boxing?
Generics provide type safety and eliminate unnecessary boxing and unboxing operations.

💻 Generic Example

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
No boxing occurs because the collection stores integers directly.
Q: Give a real-world example of accidental Boxing. 
ArrayList list = new ArrayList();

list.Add(10);
ArrayList stores objects, so the integer must be boxed before being added.
Q: Why are Generics preferred over ArrayList?
  • Type Safety
  • Better Performance
  • No Boxing/Unboxing
  • Compile-Time Type Checking

ArrayList vs Generic List

Feature ArrayList List<T>
Type Safe No Yes
Boxing Required Yes No
Performance Lower Higher
Compile-Time Checking No Yes

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: How does Boxing affect application performance?
Boxing increases memory allocations on the Heap and generates additional Garbage Collection pressure. In high-throughput enterprise applications, excessive boxing can significantly impact performance and memory consumption.

Performance Recommendation

  • Prefer Generics over non-generic collections.
  • Avoid unnecessary conversions to object.
  • Use strongly typed collections.
  • Monitor boxing operations in performance-critical code.

Section 3: Strings, Constants & Dynamic Typing

5. String vs StringBuilder

  • String and StringBuilder are both used for handling text in C#.
  • The major difference is that String is immutable, whereas StringBuilder is mutable.
  • When a String is modified, a new object is created in memory.
  • StringBuilder modifies the existing object without creating new objects repeatedly.
  • StringBuilder is preferred when performing multiple string manipulations.

Real Project Example

In report generation and CSV export modules, thousands of rows may need to be concatenated into a single text output. Using StringBuilder significantly reduces memory allocations and improves performance.

String Example

string text = "Hello";

text += " World";

text += " !!!";
Each modification creates a new string object because strings are immutable.

Memory Representation

"Hello"
   ↓
"Hello World"
   ↓
"Hello World !!!"
Multiple string objects are created in memory.

StringBuilder Example

StringBuilder sb =
    new StringBuilder();

sb.Append("Hello");
sb.Append(" World");
sb.Append(" !!!");

string result = sb.ToString();
The same object is updated internally, avoiding repeated allocations.

Comparison Table

Feature String StringBuilder
Mutable No Yes
Performance Slower for modifications Faster
Memory Usage Higher Lower
Best For Fixed Text Frequent Updates

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is String immutable?
Immutability improves security, thread safety, and performance optimizations such as string interning.
Q: When should you use StringBuilder?
Use StringBuilder when performing multiple append, insert, replace, or remove operations.
Q: Is StringBuilder always better?
No. For simple or infrequent string operations, String is simpler and perfectly acceptable.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is String Interning?
String Interning stores identical string literals in a shared memory pool to reduce memory consumption. 
string a = "Hello";
string b = "Hello";

Console.WriteLine(
ReferenceEquals(a, b)
);
Output: True

6. const vs readonly

  • Both const and readonly are used to define values that should not change.
  • const values are determined at compile time.
  • readonly values are determined at runtime.
  • readonly fields can be assigned inside constructors.

const Example

public const double PI = 3.14159;
The value must be known at compile time and cannot be modified.

readonly Example

public readonly string
ApplicationName;

public Config()
{
    ApplicationName =
        "Tutorial Portal";
}
The value can be assigned during object creation but cannot be modified afterward.

Comparison Table

Feature const readonly
Assignment Time Compile Time Runtime
Can Use Constructor No Yes
Static By Default Yes No
Value Changes Never Constructor Only

Real Project Example

Application constants such as tax percentages or status codes are often declared using const. Configuration values loaded during startup are typically stored in readonly fields.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Can const be used with DateTime?
No. DateTime values are determined at runtime and therefore cannot be declared as const. 
public readonly DateTime
StartDate = DateTime.Now;
Q: Is const implicitly static?
Yes. A const field belongs to the type itself and does not require an object instance.
Q: Can readonly be static?
Yes. A field can be declared as static readonly. 
public static readonly
string ConnectionName =
    "DefaultConnection";

Interview Tip

  • Compile-Time Constant → const
  • Runtime Constant → readonly

7. var vs dynamic

  • Both var and dynamic allow developers to avoid explicitly writing data types.
  • However, they behave very differently.
  • var uses compile-time type checking.
  • dynamic uses runtime type checking.

var Example

var name = "Ashutosh";

name = "John";
The compiler determines that name is a string. 
var age = 25;

age = "Twenty Five";
Compilation Error because age is inferred as int.

dynamic Example

dynamic value = 25;

value = "Hello";

value = true;
The type can change at runtime because validation occurs during execution.

Comparison Table

Feature var dynamic
Type Checking Compile Time Runtime
Performance Faster Slower
IntelliSense Support Yes Limited
Error Detection Compile Time Runtime

Real Project Example

I commonly use var for local variables because it improves readability while maintaining type safety. I use dynamic only when interacting with COM objects, reflection, or external libraries with unknown structures.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Is var a dynamic type?
No. var is strongly typed. The compiler determines the type during compilation.
Q: Can var be initialized with null? 
var value = null;
No. The compiler cannot infer the type.
Q: When should dynamic be used?
  • Reflection
  • COM Interop
  • Dynamic JSON Structures
  • Third-Party Dynamic APIs
Q: What is the biggest disadvantage of dynamic?
Errors are detected only at runtime, making applications harder to debug and maintain.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which would you prefer in enterprise applications?
I prefer var because it preserves compile-time safety while reducing code verbosity. I use dynamic only when absolutely necessary.
  • Prefer var for maintainable code.
  • Avoid dynamic unless runtime flexibility is required.
  • Compile-time errors are always preferable to runtime errors.

Section 4: Parameters, Abstraction & Polymorphism

8. ref vs out vs in

  • ref, out, and in are parameter modifiers in C# that allow arguments to be passed by reference instead of by value.
  • ref requires the variable to be initialized before passing and allows reading and modification inside the method.
  • out does not require initialization before passing but must be assigned within the method.
  • in passes data by reference while preventing modifications inside the method.

Real Project Example

I typically use out when a method needs to return multiple values and in when passing large read-only structures to improve performance while preventing accidental changes.

ref Example

public void UpdateValue(ref int number)
{
    number += 10;
}

int value = 5;

UpdateValue(ref value);

Console.WriteLine(value);
Output: 15

out Example

public bool TryGetUser(out string userName)
{
    userName = "Ashutosh";
    return true;
}

Usage

string userName;

TryGetUser(out userName);

in Example

public void Display(in int number)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);

    // number = 20; ❌ Not Allowed
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the difference between ref and out?
ref requires initialization before the method call, while out does not. 
int num = 10;
Update(ref num);
int num;
GetValue(out num);
Q: When is out commonly used?
Methods such as TryParse use out parameters to return parsed values. 
int.TryParse("100", out int result);
Q: Why use in?
To avoid copying large value types while ensuring the method cannot modify them.
Q: Are ref and out passed by reference?
Yes. Both pass the memory reference of the variable.
Q: Can ref parameters be optional?
No. The caller must explicitly use the ref keyword.

9. Abstract Class vs Interface

  • Both Abstract Classes and Interfaces are used to achieve abstraction.
  • An Abstract Class can contain both implemented and abstract members.
  • An Interface defines a contract that implementing classes must follow.
  • Abstract Classes are ideal for shared functionality, while Interfaces are ideal for capabilities and contracts.

Real Project Example

I use Abstract Classes when multiple implementations share common logic and Interfaces when supporting Dependency Injection and multiple implementations.

Abstract Class Example

public abstract class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Save()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee Saved");
    }

    public abstract decimal CalculateSalary();
}

Implementation

public class PermanentEmployee : Employee
{
    public override decimal CalculateSalary()
    {
        return 50000;
    }
}

Interface Example

public interface IEmailService
{
    Task SendEmailAsync();
}

Implementation

public class EmailService : IEmailService
{
    public async Task SendEmailAsync()
    {
    }
}

Comparison Table

Feature Abstract Class Interface
Constructors Yes No
Implemented Methods Yes Limited (C# 8+)
Fields Yes No
Multiple Inheritance No Yes

Follow-up Questions

Q: Can an Abstract Class have constructors?
Yes. 
protected Employee()
{
}
Q: Can an Interface have constructors?
No. Interfaces cannot contain constructors.
Q: Can a class implement multiple Interfaces? 
public class UserService :
    IUserService,
    ILogger,
    IAuditable
{
}

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why do most ASP.NET Core applications prefer Interfaces?
Dependency Injection depends on abstractions, making Interfaces ideal for testing, replacement, and extensibility. 
builder.Services.AddScoped<
    IUserService,
    UserService>();

10. Method Overloading vs Method Overriding

  • Method Overloading means multiple methods share the same name but have different parameter lists.
  • Method Overriding means a derived class provides a new implementation for a base class method.
  • Overloading supports Compile-Time Polymorphism.
  • Overriding supports Runtime Polymorphism.

Method Overloading Example

public class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }

    public int Add(int a, int b, int c)
    {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

Method Overriding Example

public class Animal
{
    public virtual void Speak()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Animal Sound");
    }
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void Speak()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Comparison Table

Feature Overloading Overriding
Inheritance Required No Yes
Resolution Time Compile Time Runtime
Polymorphism Type Static Dynamic

Follow-up Questions

Q: Can return type alone differentiate overloaded methods?
No. This causes a compilation error. 
int Get();
string Get();
Q: Which OOP principle does Overriding support?
Polymorphism.

11. Virtual vs Override vs New

  • virtual allows a base method to be overridden.
  • override replaces the base implementation.
  • new hides the base implementation instead of overriding it.
  • override should generally be preferred because it preserves polymorphic behavior.

virtual Example

public class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee Working");
    }
}

override Example

public class Manager : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Manager Working");
    }
}

Usage

Employee emp = new Manager();

emp.Work();
Output: Manager Working

new Example

public class Manager : Employee
{
    public new void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Manager Working");
    }
}

Usage

Employee emp = new Manager();

emp.Work();
Output: Employee Working
The base method is hidden, not overridden.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the purpose of virtual?
It indicates that a method can be overridden by derived classes.
Q: What happens if override is used without virtual?
Compilation Error. The base method must be virtual, abstract, or already overridden.
Q: Which keyword supports runtime polymorphism?
override
Q: Which keyword should generally be preferred?
override because it preserves polymorphic behavior.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Explain the difference between method hiding and method overriding.
Method overriding uses runtime polymorphism, while method hiding uses the compile-time type to determine which method is executed. 
Employee emp = new Manager();

emp.Work();
With override → Manager Working With new → Employee Working

Section 5: Modern C# Features

12. Extension Methods

  • Extension Methods allow us to add new functionality to an existing class without modifying its source code or creating a derived class.
  • They are defined as static methods inside a static class.
  • The first parameter uses the this keyword to specify the type being extended.
  • Extension Methods improve code reusability and readability.

Real Project Example

Suppose multiple APIs need to format user names consistently. Instead of duplicating formatting logic throughout the application, we can create a reusable Extension Method.

💻 Extension Method Example

public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static string ToTitleCase(
        this string value)
    {
        return CultureInfo
            .CurrentCulture
            .TextInfo
            .ToTitleCase(value);
    }
}

Usage

string name =
    "ashutosh parmar";

string result =
    name.ToTitleCase();
Output: Ashutosh Parmar

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why are Extension Methods useful?
  • Improve code readability
  • Promote reusability
  • Avoid modifying existing classes
  • Reduce duplicate code
Q: Can Extension Methods access private members?
No. Extension Methods can only access public members of the target class.
Q: Why must Extension Methods be static?
Because they are resolved by the compiler and are not actual instance methods.
Q: Where are Extension Methods heavily used?
LINQ is built extensively using Extension Methods. 
users.Where(x => x.IsActive)
     .OrderBy(x => x.Name)
     .ToList();
Q: What happens if the original class already contains the same method?
The actual class method gets priority over the Extension Method.

13. Delegates

  • A Delegate is a type-safe function pointer.
  • It stores references to one or more methods.
  • Delegates allow methods to be passed as parameters and executed dynamically.
  • They form the foundation of Events, LINQ, Lambda Expressions, and many ASP.NET Core features.

Real Project Example

Suppose an application supports multiple payment methods. Delegates can dynamically decide which payment method should execute.

💻 Delegate Definition

public delegate void
PaymentProcessor(decimal amount);

Methods

public static void
ProcessCreditCard(decimal amount)
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        $"Credit Card Payment:
        {amount}");
}

public static void
ProcessUPI(decimal amount)
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        $"UPI Payment:
        {amount}");
}

Usage

PaymentProcessor payment =
    ProcessCreditCard;

payment(1000);
Output: Credit Card Payment: 1000

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why are Delegates called type-safe function pointers?
Because they can only reference methods whose signatures match the delegate definition.
Q: Can a Delegate point to multiple methods?
Yes. This is called a Multicast Delegate. 
payment += ProcessUPI;
Q: What is the difference between Delegate and Interface?
Delegate Interface
Represents a method Represents a contract
Encapsulates behavior Defines structure
Q: What are built-in delegates? 
Action
Func
Predicate
Q: What is Action?
Used when a method returns void. 
Action<string> display;
Q: What is Func?
Used when a method returns a value. 
Func<int,int,int> add;
Q: What is Predicate?
Used when a method returns a boolean value. 
Predicate<int> isEven;

14. Events

  • Events allow one object to notify other objects when something important happens.
  • Events are built on top of Delegates.
  • They follow the Publisher-Subscriber pattern.
  • Events help create loosely coupled and maintainable systems.

Real Project Example

When an order is placed, multiple actions may occur such as sending emails, updating inventory, or generating invoices. Events allow these actions to be triggered independently.

Publisher

public class OrderService
{
    public event Action
        OrderPlaced;

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(
            "Order Placed");

        OrderPlaced?.Invoke();
    }
}

Subscriber

OrderService service =
    new OrderService();

service.OrderPlaced += () =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        "Email Sent");
};

service.PlaceOrder();
Output:
Order Placed
Email Sent

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the difference between Event and Delegate?
  • Delegate → Anyone can invoke it.
  • Event → Only the publisher can invoke it.
  • Events provide better encapsulation.
Q: What pattern do Events follow?
Publisher-Subscriber Pattern.
Q: Why use Events?
To decouple components. The publisher does not need to know who is listening.
Q: What is EventHandler?
A built-in delegate commonly used for events. 
public event EventHandler
    UserCreated;
Q: Can multiple subscribers listen to the same Event?
Yes. A single event can notify multiple subscribers.

15. Lambda Expressions

  • Lambda Expressions provide a concise way to write anonymous functions.
  • They simplify code and improve readability.
  • Lambdas are heavily used with LINQ, Delegates, and asynchronous programming.
  • They are one of the most frequently used features in modern C# development.

Real Project Example

I frequently use Lambda Expressions when filtering, sorting, and transforming collections using LINQ.

Traditional Method

public bool IsActive(User user)
{
    return user.IsActive;
}

Lambda Equivalent

user => user.IsActive

LINQ Example

var activeUsers =
    users.Where(
        user => user.IsActive);

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the syntax of a Lambda Expression? 
(parameters) => expression
x => x * 2
Q: Why are Lambdas useful?
  • Less Code
  • Better Readability
  • LINQ Support
  • Functional Programming Support
Q: Are Lambda Expressions Delegates?
Lambda Expressions are typically compiled into Delegates.
Q: Can Lambdas contain multiple statements? 
(x) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(x);

    return x * 2;
}
Q: Where are Lambdas commonly used?
  • LINQ
  • Delegates
  • Events
  • Async Programming

16. Generics

  • Generics allow classes, methods, interfaces, and collections to work with different data types while maintaining type safety.
  • They eliminate the need for explicit casting.
  • They improve performance by avoiding Boxing and Unboxing.
  • Generics are heavily used throughout .NET and ASP.NET Core.

Real Project Example

I frequently use Generics when building repositories, services, utility classes, and collections that must support multiple entity types.

Without Generics

ArrayList items =
    new ArrayList();

items.Add(100);

int number =
    (int)items[0];
  • Type Casting Required
  • Boxing/Unboxing
  • Potential Runtime Errors

With Generics

List<int> items =
    new List<int>();

items.Add(100);

int number = items[0];
  • Type Safety
  • Better Performance
  • Compile-Time Validation

Generic Class Example

public class Repository<T>
{
    public void Add(T entity)
    {
    }
}

Usage

Repository<User>
    userRepo =
    new Repository<User>();

Repository<Product>
    productRepo =
    new Repository<Product>();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Generics?
  • Type Safety
  • Better Performance
  • Reusability
  • No Casting
Q: What problem do Generics solve?
They remove the need for storing everything as object and eliminate unnecessary casting.
Q: How do Generics improve performance?
They prevent Boxing and Unboxing. 
List<int>
instead of 
ArrayList
Q: What are Generic Constraints?
Constraints restrict which types can be used as generic arguments. 
public class Repository<T>
    where T : class
{
}
Q: Common Generic Constraints? 
where T : class

where T : struct

where T : new()

where T : BaseClass

where T : IInterface
Q: Where are Generics used in .NET? 
List<T>

Dictionary<TKey,TValue>

Task<T>

IEnumerable<T>

DbSet<T>

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is Repository<T> commonly used in enterprise applications?
A single generic repository can work with multiple entities, reducing duplicate code and improving maintainability. 
Repository<User>

Repository<Order>

Repository<Product>

Quick Revision Table

Topic Key Point
Extension Methods Add functionality without modifying a class
Delegates Type-safe function pointers
Events Publisher-Subscriber pattern built on Delegates
Lambda Expressions Anonymous functions
Generics Type safety and code reusability

Section 6: Exception Handling, Resource Management & Garbage Collection

17. Exception Handling

  • Exception Handling is a mechanism used to handle runtime errors gracefully without crashing the application.
  • It allows applications to recover from unexpected situations and provide meaningful error information.
  • C# provides try, catch, finally, and throw keywords for exception handling.
  • Proper exception handling improves application reliability, maintainability, and debugging.

Interview Answer

Exception Handling enables developers to catch runtime errors and handle them appropriately. Instead of allowing the application to terminate unexpectedly, we can log the error, display a friendly message, or perform recovery actions.

Real Project Example

When calling external APIs, network failures, timeouts, or invalid responses may occur. Exception handling allows the application to log the issue and respond gracefully instead of crashing.

💻 Basic Exception Handling Example

try
{
    int number = 10;
    int result = number / 0;
}
catch (DivideByZeroException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        ex.Message);
}

Using Finally Block

try
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        "Processing...");
}
catch(Exception ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        ex.Message);
}
finally
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        "Cleanup Code");
}
The finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception occurs.

Throwing Exceptions

public void ProcessOrder(
    decimal amount)
{
    if(amount <= 0)
    {
        throw new Exception(
            "Invalid Amount");
    }
}

Exception Hierarchy

Exception
│
├── SystemException
│   ├── NullReferenceException
│   ├── IndexOutOfRangeException
│   ├── DivideByZeroException
│   └── InvalidOperationException
│
└── ApplicationException

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the difference between throw and throw ex?
  • throw preserves the original stack trace.
  • throw ex resets the stack trace.
  • In production applications, throw is generally preferred.
catch(Exception ex)
{
    throw;
}
Q: What is a custom exception?
A custom exception is a user-defined exception class created to represent specific business errors. 
public class
InvalidOrderException
    : Exception
{
    public InvalidOrderException(
        string message)
        : base(message)
    {
    }
}
Q: Should exceptions be used for validation?
No. Validation errors should generally be handled through validation logic rather than exceptions because exceptions are expensive operations.
Q: Why catch specific exceptions?
Specific exception handling allows targeted recovery and better debugging compared to catching generic exceptions.
Q: Can multiple catch blocks be used?
Yes. Multiple catch blocks can handle different exception types separately. 
try
{
}
catch(NullReferenceException ex)
{
}
catch(Exception ex)
{
}

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is Exception Handling best practice in ASP.NET Core?
