Use centralized exception handling middleware to capture, log, and standardize error responses across the entire application. 
app.UseExceptionHandler(
    "/Error");

18. IDisposable

  • IDisposable is an interface used to release unmanaged resources explicitly.
  • It contains a single method named Dispose().
  • Garbage Collection handles managed memory, but unmanaged resources require explicit cleanup.
  • Examples include database connections, file handles, network streams, and unmanaged memory.

Interview Answer

IDisposable provides a mechanism to release unmanaged resources when they are no longer needed. This prevents resource leaks and improves application stability.

Real Project Example

Database connections should be closed immediately after use. Relying solely on Garbage Collection can keep connections open longer than necessary and exhaust connection pools.

💻 IDisposable Example

public class FileManager
    : IDisposable
{
    public void Dispose()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(
            "Resources Released");
    }
}

Using IDisposable

using(FileManager manager =
    new FileManager())
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        "Working...");
}
Dispose() is automatically called when execution exits the using block.

Using Statement Flow

Create Object
      ↓
Use Resource
      ↓
Dispose()
      ↓
Resource Released

Common IDisposable Objects

Type Reason
SqlConnection Database Connection
FileStream File Handle
StreamReader File Resource
HttpClientHandler Network Resources
MemoryStream Memory Management

Follow-up Questions

Q: What happens if Dispose is not called?
Resources may remain allocated longer than necessary, potentially causing memory leaks, locked files, or exhausted database connections.
Q: What is the difference between Dispose and Finalize?
Dispose Finalize
Manual Cleanup Automatic Cleanup
Deterministic Non-Deterministic
Faster Slower
IDisposable Garbage Collector
Q: What does using actually do?
The compiler automatically converts a using block into a try/finally block and calls Dispose() inside finally. 
try
{
}
finally
{
    resource.Dispose();
}
Q: Can Dispose be called multiple times?
Yes. Well-designed Dispose implementations should safely handle multiple calls.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is IDisposable important in enterprise applications?
Enterprise applications frequently work with files, databases, streams, and network resources. Proper disposal prevents resource leaks and improves scalability.

19. Garbage Collection (GC)

  • Garbage Collection is an automatic memory management feature of .NET.
  • It identifies and removes objects that are no longer being used.
  • GC helps prevent memory leaks and simplifies application development.
  • Developers do not need to manually free managed memory.

Interview Answer

The Garbage Collector automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable by the application. This reduces memory management complexity and improves application reliability.

Real Project Example

In a web application handling thousands of requests, many temporary objects are created. Garbage Collection automatically cleans up these unused objects and returns memory to the application.

💻 Example

User user =
    new User();

user = null;
Once no references point to the object, it becomes eligible for Garbage Collection.

Generational Garbage Collection

Generation 0
     ↓
Generation 1
     ↓
Generation 2
.NET uses Generational Garbage Collection because most objects have short lifetimes.
Generation Description
Gen 0 Short-lived Objects
Gen 1 Medium-lived Objects
Gen 2 Long-lived Objects

GC Process

Create Object
      ↓
Use Object
      ↓
Reference Removed
      ↓
GC Marks Object
      ↓
GC Frees Memory

Follow-up Questions

Q: Can we force Garbage Collection?
Yes, using GC.Collect(), but it is generally discouraged because the runtime knows better when collection should occur. 
GC.Collect();
Q: What is Managed Memory?
Memory allocated and managed by the CLR and Garbage Collector.
Q: Does GC clean unmanaged resources?
No. Unmanaged resources should be released using IDisposable.
Q: What triggers Garbage Collection?
  • Memory Pressure
  • Low Available Memory
  • Application Activity
  • Runtime Optimization Decisions
Q: What is a Memory Leak in .NET?
A memory leak occurs when objects remain referenced and therefore cannot be collected by the Garbage Collector. 
static List<User>
    cache = new();
Objects stored indefinitely in such collections may never become eligible for collection.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is the relationship between IDisposable and Garbage Collection?
Garbage Collection handles managed memory automatically, while IDisposable handles unmanaged resource cleanup. Both work together to ensure efficient memory and resource management.

Quick Revision Table

Topic Key Point
Exception Handling Gracefully handle runtime errors
IDisposable Release unmanaged resources
Garbage Collection Automatic memory management

Section 7: Multithreading & Asynchronous Programming

20. Task vs Thread

  • A Thread is the smallest unit of execution managed by the operating system.
  • A Task is a higher-level abstraction introduced by .NET for asynchronous and parallel programming.
  • Tasks typically run on ThreadPool threads and provide built-in support for cancellation, continuations, exception handling, and return values.
  • Modern .NET applications generally prefer Tasks because they are more scalable and easier to manage.

Interview Answer

A Thread represents an actual OS-level execution unit, whereas a Task represents an asynchronous operation. Tasks abstract thread management and allow developers to focus on business logic rather than thread lifecycle management.

Real Project Example

Suppose an API needs to generate a report in the background.

Using Thread

Thread thread = new Thread(() =>
{
    GenerateReport();
});

thread.Start();

Using Task

Task.Run(() =>
{
    GenerateReport();
});
The Task approach is preferred because .NET manages thread allocation efficiently using the ThreadPool.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is a Thread?
A Thread is an actual operating system execution unit with its own stack, execution context, and scheduling overhead.
Q: What is a Task?
A Task represents an asynchronous operation and may use a ThreadPool thread, background thread, or I/O completion port depending on the operation. 
ThreadPool Thread
Background Thread
I/O Completion Port
Q: Which is preferred in modern .NET?
  • Easier to write
  • Better performance
  • Improved scalability
  • Built-in async support
Q: Does every Task create a new Thread?
No. Most Tasks use existing ThreadPool threads rather than creating new threads.
Q: Which consumes more resources?
Threads consume more resources because creating a new thread is expensive.
Q: Can a Task return a value? 
Task<int> GetTotalAsync()
{
    return Task.FromResult(100);
}
Q: Can a Thread return a value directly?
No. Additional synchronization mechanisms are required.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is Task preferred in ASP.NET Core?
ASP.NET Core applications handle many concurrent requests. Creating dedicated threads for every request would be expensive. Tasks efficiently utilize the ThreadPool and improve application throughput.

21. Async/Await Deep Dive

  • async and await simplify asynchronous programming in C#.
  • They prevent threads from being blocked during long-running I/O operations.
  • Common use cases include database calls, API requests, and file operations.
  • Async programming improves scalability in ASP.NET Core applications.

Interview Answer

Async and Await allow applications to perform non-blocking operations. While waiting for external resources such as databases or APIs, the request thread can be returned to the ThreadPool and used for other work.

Real Project Example

public async Task<List<User>>
GetUsersAsync()
{
    return await _context.Users
        .ToListAsync();
}
While SQL Server processes the query, the thread is released back to the ThreadPool and can serve other requests.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What does async do?
Marks a method as asynchronous. 
public async Task
GetDataAsync()
{
}
Q: What does await do?
Pauses execution until an asynchronous operation completes. 
await GetDataAsync();
Q: Can we use await without async?
No. This causes a compiler error.
Q: Can we use async without await?
Yes, but the compiler usually generates a warning.
Q: Does async create a new Thread?
No. Async is about non-blocking operations, not thread creation.
Q: What is the benefit of async in Web APIs? 
Without Async

Request Thread
      ↓
Wait For Database
      ↓
Blocked
With Async

Request Thread
      ↓
Database Call Starts
      ↓
Thread Released
      ↓
Database Completes
      ↓
Thread Resumes
This improves application scalability and throughput.
Q: What is an I/O Bound operation?
  • Database Calls
  • API Requests
  • File Access
Async programming is highly beneficial for I/O-bound operations.
Q: What is a CPU Bound operation?
  • Image Processing
  • Encryption
  • Large Calculations
Async alone may not improve performance for CPU-bound work.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens internally when await is encountered?
  • Method execution pauses.
  • Current state is captured.
  • Thread is released.
  • Operation continues asynchronously.
  • Execution resumes when the operation completes.
The compiler implements this behavior using a generated state machine.

22. ThreadPool

  • ThreadPool is a collection of reusable worker threads managed by the CLR.
  • It reduces the overhead of creating and destroying threads repeatedly.
  • Most Tasks execute using ThreadPool threads.
  • Thread reuse improves performance and scalability.

Interview Answer

The ThreadPool provides reusable worker threads that execute background work. Instead of creating new threads for every operation, .NET efficiently reuses existing threads.

Real Project Example

Task.Run(() =>
{
    ProcessData();
});
Task
  ↓
ThreadPool
  ↓
Worker Thread
No new thread is typically created.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use ThreadPool?
  • Better performance
  • Reduced memory usage
  • Thread reuse
  • Improved scalability
Q: What is the disadvantage of creating Threads manually?
  • Expensive creation cost
  • Higher memory usage
  • More context switching
Q: Can ThreadPool threads be reused?
Yes. Thread reuse is the primary purpose of ThreadPool.
Q: Does ASP.NET Core use ThreadPool?
Yes. ASP.NET Core heavily relies on ThreadPool threads.
Q: How can we queue work to ThreadPool? 
ThreadPool
    .QueueUserWorkItem(
        state =>
        {
            Console.WriteLine(
                "Work");
        });

23. Parallel Programming

  • Parallel Programming executes multiple operations simultaneously.
  • It utilizes multiple CPU cores.
  • Its goal is maximum CPU utilization.
  • Unlike async programming, it focuses on CPU-bound workloads.

Interview Answer

Parallel Programming improves performance by distributing work across multiple processor cores and executing tasks simultaneously.

Real Project Example

Without Parallelism

foreach(var record in records)
{
    Process(record);
}

With Parallelism

Parallel.ForEach(
    records,
    record =>
    {
        Process(record);
    });
Multiple CPU cores process records simultaneously.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between Async and Parallel Programming?
Async Parallel
I/O Bound CPU Bound
Non-Blocking Multi-Core Execution
Q: What is Parallel.ForEach?
Processes collection items concurrently. 
Parallel.ForEach(
    items,
    item =>
    {
    });
Q: What are the risks of Parallel Programming?
  • Race Conditions
  • Deadlocks
  • Synchronization Issues
Q: When should Parallel Programming be used?
  • Data Processing
  • Image Processing
  • Scientific Calculations
Q: Should Parallel.ForEach be used for database calls?
Generally no. Database calls are I/O-bound and Async/Await is preferred.

24. CancellationToken

  • CancellationToken provides a cooperative way to cancel ongoing asynchronous operations.
  • It helps save resources and improve responsiveness.
  • Cancellation is not forced.
  • The executing code must respect the token.

Interview Answer

CancellationToken allows applications to stop unnecessary work when an operation is no longer needed.

Real Project Example

public async Task
GetDataAsync(
    CancellationToken token)
{
    await Task.Delay(
        10000,
        token);
}
If a client disconnects, the operation can be cancelled to save resources.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use CancellationToken?
  • Save resources
  • Improve responsiveness
  • Stop unnecessary work
Q: How do we create one? 
CancellationTokenSource cts =
    new CancellationTokenSource();
Q: How do we cancel? 
cts.Cancel();
Q: How do we check cancellation? 
token
    .ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
Q: Is cancellation forced?
No. CancellationToken uses cooperative cancellation.

25. ConfigureAwait

  • ConfigureAwait controls whether an awaited operation resumes on the original synchronization context.
  • It was extremely important in ASP.NET Framework.
  • Its benefits are much smaller in ASP.NET Core.
  • It remains useful when building reusable libraries.

Interview Answer

ConfigureAwait determines whether execution should continue on the original synchronization context after an awaited operation completes.

Real Project Example

await GetDataAsync()
    .ConfigureAwait(false);
The continuation may execute on any available thread.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why was ConfigureAwait(false) important in ASP.NET Framework?
  • Avoided synchronization context capture
  • Reduced performance overhead
  • Prevented deadlocks
Q: Is ConfigureAwait(false) required in ASP.NET Core?
Usually no. ASP.NET Core does not use the same SynchronizationContext model as ASP.NET Framework.
Q: Where is ConfigureAwait(false) still useful?
Reusable library code where the caller's synchronization context is unknown.
Q: Can ConfigureAwait(false) improve performance?
Slightly, by avoiding context capture in certain scenarios.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why do many developers still use ConfigureAwait(false) everywhere?
Because it was considered a best practice in ASP.NET Framework. In ASP.NET Core, many teams reserve it primarily for reusable library code.

Section 8: ASP.NET Core Fundamentals

26. What is ASP.NET Core?

  • ASP.NET Core is a cross-platform, open-source, high-performance web framework developed by Microsoft.
  • It is used to build modern web applications, REST APIs, microservices, and cloud-native applications.
  • It runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
  • It includes built-in support for Dependency Injection, Middleware, Configuration, Logging, Authentication, and Routing.

Interview Answer

ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's modern web development framework for building scalable and high-performance applications. It is cross-platform, cloud-friendly, and includes many enterprise-grade features out of the box. In my projects, I primarily use ASP.NET Core to build REST APIs consumed by React applications and external systems.

Real Project Example

In one of my projects, I built a reporting API using ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core. The API retrieved data from SQL Server, applied business rules, generated report data, and exposed REST endpoints consumed by a React frontend.

💻 API Controller Example

[ApiController]
[Route("api/users")]
public class UsersController
    : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult GetUsers()
    {
        return Ok();
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why ASP.NET Core over ASP.NET Framework?
ASP.NET Core ASP.NET Framework
Cross-platform Windows Only
Better Performance Slower
Built-in DI Limited DI
Cloud Friendly Less Cloud Focused
Modular Architecture Monolithic
Q: What applications can be built using ASP.NET Core?
  • REST APIs
  • Web Applications
  • Microservices
  • Cloud Applications
  • Real-Time Applications
  • Background Services
Q: Is ASP.NET Core cross-platform?
Yes. ASP.NET Core runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
Q: What server does ASP.NET Core use? 
Kestrel
Q: What are the major features of ASP.NET Core?
  • Dependency Injection
  • Middleware
  • Logging
  • Authentication
  • Routing
  • Configuration
  • Cross-Platform Support
  • High Performance

27. ASP.NET Core Request Lifecycle

  • The Request Lifecycle describes how an HTTP request travels through an ASP.NET Core application.
  • A request enters Kestrel, passes through Middleware, reaches Controllers/Endpoints, and returns a response.
  • Middleware execution order directly affects application behavior.
  • Understanding the lifecycle is essential for debugging and performance optimization.

Interview Answer

The ASP.NET Core Request Lifecycle explains how incoming requests are processed and how responses are generated. A request flows through Kestrel, Middleware, Routing, Controllers, Services, and Data Access layers before a response is sent back to the client.

Lifecycle Flow

Client Request
      ↓
Kestrel Server
      ↓
Middleware Pipeline
      ↓
Routing Middleware
      ↓
Controller/Endpoint
      ↓
Business Logic
      ↓
Response
      ↓
Middleware Pipeline
      ↓
Client

Real Project Example

User requests: 
GET /api/users
Authentication Middleware
        ↓
Logging Middleware
        ↓
Routing Middleware
        ↓
UsersController
        ↓
UserService
        ↓
Database
        ↓
Response

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the first component that receives a request?
Kestrel Server.
Q: What controls request flow?
Middleware Pipeline.
Q: Can Middleware stop a request? 
if(!authenticated)
{
    return;
}
Yes. The request may never reach the controller.
Q: Why is Middleware order important?
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Routing
Requests execute sequentially, so incorrect ordering can break application functionality.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Explain request flow in a real API. 
Request
 ↓
Kestrel
 ↓
Exception Middleware
 ↓
Authentication Middleware
 ↓
Authorization Middleware
 ↓
Routing Middleware
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service Layer
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Database
 ↓
Response

28. Middleware Deep Dive

  • Middleware is software that sits in the request processing pipeline.
  • Middleware can inspect, modify, or terminate requests and responses.
  • Each Middleware component can execute logic before and after the next Middleware.
  • Middleware is one of the most important concepts in ASP.NET Core.

Interview Answer

Middleware components form the ASP.NET Core request processing pipeline. Each component receives the HTTP request, performs some work, and optionally passes control to the next component.

Built-in Middleware Examples

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.UseRouting();

app.UseCors();

app.UseExceptionHandler();

Custom Middleware Example

public class
RequestLoggingMiddleware
{
    private readonly
        RequestDelegate _next;

    public RequestLoggingMiddleware(
        RequestDelegate next)
    {
        _next = next;
    }

    public async Task InvokeAsync(
        HttpContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(
            "Request Started");

        await _next(context);

        Console.WriteLine(
            "Request Finished");
    }
}

Registration

app.UseMiddleware<
RequestLoggingMiddleware>();

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Middleware?
A component that processes requests and responses.
Q: How many Middleware components can exist?
Unlimited. Multiple Middleware components form the request pipeline.
Q: What is RequestDelegate?
Represents the next Middleware in the pipeline. 
await _next(context);
Q: What happens if _next is not called?
The pipeline stops and the request never reaches subsequent Middleware.
Q: Difference between Use, Run, and Map?

Use

Passes control to the next Middleware. 
app.Use(...)

Run

Terminal Middleware. Pipeline ends. 
app.Run(...)

Map

Branches the pipeline. 
app.Map("/admin", ...)

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which Middleware order is commonly used? 
app.UseExceptionHandler();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseRouting();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();
Authentication must execute before Authorization.

29. Dependency Injection (DI) Deep Dive

  • Dependency Injection is a design pattern used to achieve loose coupling.
  • Dependencies are injected into classes instead of being created using the new keyword.
  • ASP.NET Core provides built-in Dependency Injection support.
  • DI improves maintainability, flexibility, and testability.

Interview Answer

Dependency Injection allows classes to receive dependencies from the ASP.NET Core DI Container rather than creating them directly. This reduces tight coupling and improves code quality.

Without DI

public class UserController
{
    private UserService _service =
        new UserService();
}
Problem: Tightly coupled and difficult to test.

With DI

public class UserController
{
    private readonly
        IUserService _service;

    public UserController(
        IUserService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }
}

Registration

builder.Services
       .AddScoped<IUserService,
                  UserService>();

Follow-up Questions

Q: What problem does DI solve?
Reduces tight coupling between components.
Q: Why use Interfaces with DI?
Interfaces allow multiple implementations and make testing easier. 
IUserService
Q: What are DI benefits?
  • Loose Coupling
  • Testability
  • Maintainability
  • Extensibility
Q: What type of injection is commonly used?
Constructor Injection. 
public UserController(
    IUserService service)
{
}
Q: Why avoid using new inside Controllers?
It creates tight coupling and makes unit testing difficult.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: How does ASP.NET Core resolve dependencies? 
Request
 ↓
Controller Requested
 ↓
DI Container Checks Registrations
 ↓
Creates Required Services
 ↓
Injects Dependencies
 ↓
Controller Created

30. Service Lifetimes

  • ASP.NET Core supports three service lifetimes.
  • Transient creates a new instance every time.
  • Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request.
  • Singleton creates a single instance for the application's lifetime.

Interview Answer

Service lifetimes determine how long a service instance remains alive. Choosing the correct lifetime is important for performance, memory management, and application stability.

Transient

Creates a new instance every time it is requested. 
builder.Services
       .AddTransient<IEmailService,
                     EmailService>();

Scoped

Creates one instance per HTTP request. 
builder.Services
       .AddScoped<IUserService,
                  UserService>();

Singleton

Creates a single instance for the entire application lifetime. 
builder.Services
       .AddSingleton<ICacheService,
                     CacheService>();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which lifetime is most commonly used?
Scoped. Most business services and repositories use Scoped lifetime.
Q: What lifetime does DbContext use?
Scoped. 
AddDbContext()
Q: Why shouldn't DbContext be Singleton?
  • Data Corruption
  • Thread Safety Issues
  • Entity Tracking Problems
Q: When should Singleton be used?
  • Cache Services
  • Configuration Services
  • Stateless Utilities
Q: Which lifetime creates the most objects?
Transient lifetime because a new instance is created on every injection.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Can a Singleton depend on a Scoped service?
No. This causes a runtime error because a Singleton cannot consume a Scoped dependency. 
Cannot consume scoped service
from singleton

Section 9: ASP.NET Core Infrastructure & Configuration

31. Kestrel

  • Kestrel is the cross-platform, high-performance web server used by ASP.NET Core applications.
  • It receives HTTP requests, handles network communication, and forwards requests to the ASP.NET Core pipeline.
  • It supports Windows, Linux, and macOS.
  • In production environments, Kestrel is commonly hosted behind a reverse proxy.

Interview Answer

Kestrel is the default web server used by ASP.NET Core applications. It is designed for high performance and cross-platform support. In production deployments, Kestrel is typically hosted behind reverse proxies such as Nginx, Apache, or IIS for additional security, SSL termination, and load balancing capabilities.

Real Project Example

When a React application calls an API endpoint, the request first reaches Kestrel, which forwards it through the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline before reaching controllers and services. 
React App
    ↓
Kestrel
    ↓
Middleware
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
Database
    ↓
Response

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Kestrel?
Kestrel is the default web server for ASP.NET Core applications.
Q: Is Kestrel cross-platform?
Yes. It runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
Q: Can Kestrel directly serve requests?
Yes. However, in production environments it is commonly placed behind a reverse proxy.
Q: Why use a reverse proxy?
  • Load Balancing
  • SSL Termination
  • Security
  • Request Filtering
Q: Does every ASP.NET Core application use Kestrel?
Yes. Kestrel is the default web server used by ASP.NET Core.

32. Routing

  • Routing is the process of matching incoming HTTP requests to endpoints.
  • ASP.NET Core uses Endpoint Routing to determine which code handles a request.
  • Routing can be configured using Conventional Routing or Attribute Routing.
  • Attribute Routing is the preferred approach for Web APIs.

Interview Answer

Routing maps incoming URLs to controller actions, minimal APIs, or endpoints. ASP.NET Core uses Endpoint Routing to efficiently determine which handler should process a request.

Real Project Example

[ApiController]
[Route("api/users")]
public class UsersController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult GetUsers()
    {
        return Ok();
    }
}
Request: 
GET /api/users
Routing maps the request to: 
GetUsers()

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Routing?
A mechanism that maps URLs to endpoints.
Q: What are the types of Routing?

Conventional Routing

app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "default",
    pattern:
    "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}");

Attribute Routing

[Route("api/users")]
Most commonly used in Web APIs.
Q: What is Endpoint Routing?
Introduced in ASP.NET Core 3.0, Endpoint Routing provides a unified routing system.
Q: What does id? mean? 
{id?}
It indicates an optional route parameter.
Q: Which routing approach is preferred for APIs? 
[HttpGet("{id}")]
Attribute Routing is preferred because routes are defined close to controller actions.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Difference between Conventional and Attribute Routing?
  • Conventional Routing is centralized.
  • Attribute Routing is defined directly on controllers and actions.
  • Modern Web APIs primarily use Attribute Routing.

33. Model Binding

  • Model Binding automatically maps request data to method parameters and models.
  • It supports Route Values, Query Strings, Form Data, Headers, and Request Body.
  • It eliminates manual extraction of request values.
  • It improves productivity and reduces boilerplate code.

Interview Answer

Model Binding automatically converts incoming HTTP request data into C# objects or action parameters. This simplifies controller code and reduces manual parsing logic.

Real Project Example

POST /api/users
Request Body: 
{
  "name":"Ashutosh",
  "email":"ash@gmail.com"
}
public class CreateUserRequest
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

```
public string Email { get; set; }
```

}
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult CreateUser(
    CreateUserRequest request)
{
    return Ok();
}
ASP.NET Core automatically populates the CreateUserRequest object.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Model Binding?
Automatic mapping of request data to objects and parameters.
Q: What sources can Model Binding use?
  • Route Values
  • Query String
  • Form Data
  • Headers
  • Request Body
Q: What does [FromBody] do? 
public IActionResult Create(
    [FromBody] User user)
{
}
Reads data from the request body.
Q: What does [FromQuery] do? 
public IActionResult Search(
    [FromQuery] string name)
{
}
Reads values from query strings.
Q: What does [FromRoute] do? 
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public IActionResult Get(
    [FromRoute] int id)
{
}
Reads values from route parameters.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens if Model Binding fails?
ASP.NET Core automatically populates ModelState and typically returns a 400 Bad Request response when using the ApiController attribute. 
ModelState

34. Filters

  • Filters execute logic before or after request processing stages.
  • They help implement cross-cutting concerns.
  • Common use cases include Logging, Validation, Authorization, and Exception Handling.
  • Filters prevent code duplication across controllers.

Interview Answer

Filters provide a mechanism for executing reusable logic before or after controller actions. They are commonly used for validation, logging, authorization, and exception handling.

Real Project Example

public class LoggingFilter
    : ActionFilterAttribute
{
    public override void OnActionExecuting(
        ActionExecutingContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Action Started");
    }
}
Usage: 
[LoggingFilter]
public IActionResult GetUsers()
{
    return Ok();
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Types of Filters?
  • Authorization Filter
  • Resource Filter
  • Action Filter
  • Exception Filter
  • Result Filter
Q: Difference between Middleware and Filters?
Middleware Filters
Entire Request Pipeline MVC Pipeline Only
Q: Which executes first?
Middleware executes before Filters.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When would you use Middleware vs Filters?
  • Middleware: Logging, Authentication, Global Exception Handling
  • Filters: Validation, Action Execution Logic, Controller-Specific Concerns

35. Configuration

  • Configuration provides centralized application settings management.
  • Settings can come from multiple sources.
  • ASP.NET Core supports layered configuration providers.
  • Configuration values can be overridden by higher-priority sources.

Interview Answer

Configuration in ASP.NET Core allows applications to retrieve settings from sources such as appsettings.json, environment variables, Azure Key Vault, and command-line arguments.

Configuration Sources

  • appsettings.json
  • Environment Variables
  • Command Line Arguments
  • Azure Key Vault
  • User Secrets

Real Project Example

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "DefaultConnection":
      "Server=SQL01;Database=AppDb"
  }
}
public class UserService
{
    private readonly IConfiguration _config;

```
public UserService(
    IConfiguration config)
{
    _config = config;
}
```

}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is IConfiguration?
Interface used to access configuration values.
Q: How do you read a configuration value? 
var connectionString =
_config["ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection"];
Q: Which file is commonly used? 
appsettings.json
Q: Can environment variables override appsettings?
Yes. Environment variables have higher priority.
Q: Why avoid hardcoding configuration?
Configuration changes should not require recompilation or code modifications.

36. Options Pattern

  • The Options Pattern provides strongly typed configuration access.
  • Configuration values are mapped to C# classes.
  • It improves readability, maintainability, and type safety.
  • It eliminates magic strings throughout the application.

Interview Answer

The Options Pattern maps configuration sections directly to strongly typed classes, making configuration management cleaner and safer.

37. Logging

  • Logging is the process of recording application events, warnings, errors, and diagnostic information.
  • ASP.NET Core provides built-in logging support through ILogger.
  • Proper logging helps monitor application health and troubleshoot production issues.
  • Logs are essential for debugging, auditing, and performance monitoring.

Interview Answer

Logging is used to track application behavior, capture errors, and provide diagnostic information. ASP.NET Core includes a built-in logging abstraction through ILogger, allowing applications to write logs to multiple destinations such as Console, Files, Application Insights, Serilog, and other providers.

Real Project Example

In production APIs, logging is commonly used to track request flow, user actions, external API calls, and exceptions. 
public class UserService
{
    private readonly ILogger<UserService>
        _logger;

    public UserService(
        ILogger<UserService> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }

    public void CreateUser()
    {
        _logger.LogInformation(
            "User creation started");
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is ILogger?
ILogger is ASP.NET Core's built-in logging abstraction used to write logs independent of the actual logging provider. 
ILogger<T>
Q: Common Log Levels? 
Trace
Debug
Information
Warning
Error
Critical
Q: Difference between Warning and Error?
  • Warning: Unexpected condition but application continues running.
  • Error: An operation failed and requires attention.
Q: Why should exceptions be logged?
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Stack Trace Information
  • Request Details
  • Production Troubleshooting
Q: Popular logging libraries?
  • Serilog
  • NLog
  • log4net

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is Structured Logging?
Structured logging stores log data in a searchable format rather than plain text.

❌ Bad Example

_logger.LogInformation(
    $"User {userId} created");

✅ Good Example

_logger.LogInformation(
    "User {UserId} created",
    userId);
  • Searchable Logs
  • Better Analytics
  • Works Well With Monitoring Tools
  • Improved Query Performance

Section 10: ASP.NET Core Security & Authentication

38. Authentication vs Authorization

  • Authentication identifies who the user is.
  • Authorization determines what the user is allowed to do.
  • Authentication always happens before Authorization.
  • Both are essential for securing APIs and applications.

Interview Answer

Authentication verifies a user's identity, while Authorization determines whether that authenticated user has permission to access a resource or perform an action.

Real Project Example

User Login
    ↓
Authentication
    ↓
Identity Verified
    ↓
Authorization
    ↓
Access Granted/Denied

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Authentication?
The process of verifying a user's identity.
Q: What is Authorization?
The process of determining whether an authenticated user has permission to access a resource.
Q: Which occurs first?
Authentication always occurs before Authorization.
Q: Can Authorization happen without Authentication?
No. The system must know who the user is before determining permissions.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens when an unauthenticated user accesses a protected endpoint?
The request receives a 401 Unauthorized response. 
HTTP 401 Unauthorized

39. JWT Authentication

  • JWT stands for JSON Web Token.
  • JWT enables stateless authentication.
  • Tokens contain user identity and claims.
  • JWT is widely used in modern APIs and microservices.

Interview Answer

JWT Authentication allows clients to authenticate once and use a token for subsequent requests. The server validates the token instead of maintaining session state.

JWT Flow

User Login
    ↓
Server Validates Credentials
    ↓
JWT Generated
    ↓
Client Stores Token
    ↓
Client Sends Token
    ↓
Server Validates Token
    ↓
Access Granted

Real Project Example

Authorization:
Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1Ni...

Follow-up Questions

Q: What are JWT parts? 
Header
Payload
Signature
Q: Where is JWT usually sent? 
Authorization: Bearer Token
Q: Why use JWT?
  • Stateless Authentication
  • Scalable
  • Works Well With APIs
  • Microservice Friendly
Q: Can JWT be decoded?
Yes. JWT payload can be decoded, but the signature prevents tampering.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What are common JWT security practices?
  • Use HTTPS
  • Short Expiration Times
  • Refresh Tokens
  • Strong Signing Keys
  • Validate Issuer and Audience

40. Claims-Based Authorization

  • Claims represent information about a user.
  • Authorization decisions can be based on claims.
  • Claims are commonly stored inside JWT tokens.
  • Claims-based authorization provides fine-grained access control.

Interview Answer

Claims-Based Authorization uses user claims such as Role, Department, Country, or Custom Permissions to determine access rights.

Real Project Example

{
  "sub": "101",
  "role": "Admin",
  "department": "HR"
}
The application can allow or deny access based on these claims.

Authorization Policy Example

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(
options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy(
        "AdminOnly",
        policy =>
        {
            policy.RequireClaim(
                "role",
                "Admin");
        });
});

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is a Claim?
A claim is a piece of information about a user.
Q: Examples of Claims?
  • User Id
  • Email
  • Role
  • Department
  • Country
Q: Where are Claims commonly stored?
Inside JWT tokens or authentication tickets.
Q: Why use Claims instead of Roles only?
Claims provide more detailed authorization control beyond simple role checks.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When would Claims-Based Authorization be preferred?
When authorization decisions depend on multiple user attributes such as Department, Subscription Level, Region, or Custom Permissions instead of only roles.
  • Fine-Grained Security
  • Flexible Authorization Rules
  • Works Well With JWT
  • Supports Enterprise Applications

Section 9: ASP.NET Core Web API Advanced Topics

38. What is a REST API?

  • REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style used for designing web services that communicate over HTTP.
  • A REST API exposes resources through URLs and uses standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE to perform operations on those resources.
  • REST APIs are stateless, meaning each request contains all the information needed to process it.
  • In my projects, I use ASP.NET Core Web APIs to expose business functionality that can be consumed by React applications, mobile apps, and third-party systems.

Real Project Example

User Resource endpoints: 
GET /api/users
GET /api/users/1
POST /api/users
PUT /api/users/1
DELETE /api/users/1
Each URL represents a resource.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What are REST principles?
  • Client-Server Architecture
  • Stateless Communication
  • Uniform Interface
  • Cacheable Responses
  • Layered System
Q: Why are REST APIs stateless?
Because each request contains all required information.
  • Scalability
  • Reliability
  • Simpler Architecture
Q: What is a resource in REST? 
User
Order
Product
Report
Represented through URLs.
Q: Why is REST popular?
  • Simple
  • Platform Independent
  • HTTP Based
  • Scalable

39. HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)

  • HTTP methods define the action that should be performed on a resource.
  • Each method has a specific purpose in REST APIs.

GET - Retrieve Data

GET /api/users/1

💻 Practical Code Example

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public IActionResult GetUser(int id)
{
}

POST - Create Resource

POST /api/users
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult CreateUser(
    CreateUserRequest request)
{
}

PUT - Replace Resource

PUT /api/users/1

PATCH - Partial Update

PATCH /api/users/1

DELETE - Remove Resource

DELETE /api/users/1

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between PUT and PATCH?
PUT performs a full update while PATCH performs a partial update. 
Current User:
{
  "name":"Ashutosh",
  "email":"ash@gmail.com"
}

PUT requires the complete object.

PATCH may update only:

{
  "email":"new@gmail.com"
}
Q: Which methods are idempotent?
Idempotent means repeated requests produce the same result. 
Idempotent:
GET
PUT
DELETE

Not necessarily idempotent:
POST
Q: Why should GET never modify data?
GET should be safe and cacheable. Changing data in GET violates REST principles.

40. HTTP Status Codes

  • HTTP Status Codes indicate the outcome of a request.
  • They help clients understand whether a request succeeded or failed.

Common Status Codes

Status Code Description
200 OK Request successful
201 Created Resource created successfully
204 No Content Success with no response body
400 Bad Request Invalid client request
401 Unauthorized Authentication required
403 Forbidden Authenticated but lacks permission
404 Not Found Resource does not exist
409 Conflict Request conflict
500 Internal Server Error Unexpected server error

💻 Practical Code Examples

return Ok(data);

return CreatedAtAction(...);

return NoContent();

return BadRequest();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between 401 and 403? 
401 = Not Authenticated

403 = Authenticated But Not Authorized
Q: When should 201 be returned?
After successful resource creation.
Q: When should 204 be returned?
When an operation succeeds but no content needs to be returned, such as DELETE requests.

41. Content Negotiation

  • Content Negotiation is the process by which the client and server agree on the response format.
  • The client specifies supported formats through the Accept header.
  • ASP.NET Core automatically selects the appropriate formatter.

Real Project Example

JSON Request: 
Accept: application/json

{
  "id": 1
}
XML Request: 
Accept: application/xml

<User>
  <Id>1</Id>
</User>

Follow-up Questions

Q: What header controls Content Negotiation? 
Accept
Q: What format is most common? 
JSON
Q: Why is Content Negotiation useful?
It allows the same API to support multiple client types and response formats.

42. Swagger / OpenAPI

  • Swagger is a tool that automatically generates interactive API documentation based on API definitions.
  • It allows developers to view endpoints, request models, response models, and test APIs directly from the browser.
  • Swagger improves API discoverability and reduces integration effort.

Real Project Example

Swagger setup in ASP.NET Core:

💻 Service Registration 

builder.Services.AddEndpointsApiExplorer();

builder.Services.AddSwaggerGen();

💻 Middleware Configuration 

app.UseSwagger();

app.UseSwaggerUI();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Swagger?
  • API Documentation
  • API Testing
  • Team Collaboration
Q: What is OpenAPI?
OpenAPI is the specification, while Swagger is the tool that implements the OpenAPI specification.
Q: Can Swagger generate request models?
Yes. Swagger automatically documents DTOs, request models, response models, and API endpoints.

43. API Versioning

  • API Versioning allows multiple versions of an API to coexist without breaking existing clients.
  • As APIs evolve, versioning helps maintain backward compatibility.
  • It ensures existing consumers continue working while new features are introduced.

Real Project Example

Versioned endpoints: 
/api/v1/users

/api/v2/users

💻 Controller Example 

[ApiVersion("1.0")]
[Route("api/v{version:apiVersion}/users")]
public class UsersController : ControllerBase
{
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is API Versioning important?
It prevents breaking changes from affecting existing consumers and allows APIs to evolve safely.
Q: Common Versioning Approaches?

URL Versioning

/api/v1/users

Header Versioning

api-version: 1.0

Query String Versioning

/api/users?version=1
Q: Which approach is most common?
URL Versioning is the most commonly used approach because it is simple, explicit, and easy to understand.

44. Pagination

  • Pagination divides large datasets into smaller chunks to improve performance and reduce response size.
  • Instead of returning thousands of records, APIs return a subset of records per request.
  • Pagination improves scalability and user experience.

Real Project Example

Client Request: 
GET /api/users?page=1&pageSize=20

💻 Controller Example 

[HttpGet]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetUsers(
    int page = 1,
    int pageSize = 20)
{
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Pagination?
  • Better Performance
  • Lower Memory Usage
  • Faster Responses
  • Improved Scalability
Q: What is Skip and Take?

💻 EF Core Example 

var users = await _context.Users
    .Skip((page - 1) * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
    .ToListAsync();
Q: What is the problem with returning all records?
Returning all records creates large payloads, increases memory consumption, slows responses, and impacts database performance.

45. Filtering & Sorting

  • Filtering allows clients to retrieve only relevant data.
  • Sorting controls the order of returned records.
  • These techniques improve API usability and reduce unnecessary data transfer.

Real Project Example

Filtering Request: 
GET /api/users?isActive=true
Sorting Request: 
GET /api/users?sortBy=name

💻 LINQ Example 

var users = _context.Users
    .Where(x => x.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(x => x.Name);

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why implement filtering?
Filtering reduces unnecessary data retrieval and returns only relevant information to the client.
Q: Why implement sorting?
Sorting helps return data in a meaningful and user-friendly order.
Q: Can filtering and pagination be combined?
Yes. Most production APIs combine filtering, sorting, and pagination together for optimal performance and usability. 
Filtering
Sorting
Pagination

46. Global Exception Handling

  • Global Exception Handling centralizes error handling across the application.
  • Instead of placing try-catch blocks in every controller, exceptions are handled in one location.
  • This improves maintainability, consistency, and logging.

Real Project Example

Program.cs configuration: 
app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");
Custom Middleware: 
public class ExceptionMiddleware
{
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why avoid try-catch in every controller?
Because it leads to duplicated code and makes applications harder to maintain.
Q: Benefits of Global Exception Handling?
  • Centralized Logging
  • Consistent Error Responses
  • Cleaner Controllers
  • Easier Maintenance
Q: What status code is typically returned? 
500 Internal Server Error

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What should be logged during exception handling?
  • Exception Message
  • Stack Trace
  • Request Path
  • Correlation Id

47. Rate Limiting

  • Rate Limiting restricts how many requests a client can make within a specific time period.
  • It protects APIs from abuse, accidental overload, and denial-of-service scenarios.
  • Rate limiting improves stability and resource availability.

Real Project Example

ASP.NET Core Rate Limiter Registration: 
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
});
Example Policy: 
100 Requests Per Minute

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Rate Limiting?
  • Prevent Abuse
  • Protect Resources
  • Improve Stability
  • Control Traffic
Q: What happens when the limit is exceeded? 
429 Too Many Requests
Q: Common Rate Limiting Strategies?

Fixed Window

100 Requests / Minute

Sliding Window

A more flexible approach that uses a moving time window instead of fixed intervals.

Token Bucket

Tokens are replenished over time and requests consume available tokens.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Where is Rate Limiting commonly applied?
  • Public APIs
  • Authentication Endpoints
  • Payment APIs
  • Search Endpoints
