Section 10: Entity Framework Core

48. What is Entity Framework Core?

  • Entity Framework Core (EF Core) is Microsoft's open-source Object Relational Mapper (ORM) for .NET.
  • It allows developers to work with databases using C# objects instead of writing raw SQL for every operation.
  • EF Core handles querying, inserting, updating, and deleting data while mapping database tables to C# classes.
  • In real-world projects, EF Core is commonly used with SQL Server to manage database operations, repositories, and LINQ-based queries.

Real Project Example

Without EF Core, developers manually create SQL queries and database connections. EF Core simplifies this by generating SQL automatically and mapping records to C# objects.

💻 Without EF Core

string query =
    "SELECT * FROM Users";

SqlConnection connection =
    new SqlConnection(connectionString);

💻 With EF Core

var users =
    await _context.Users.ToListAsync();

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is ORM?
ORM stands for Object Relational Mapper. It maps database tables to C# objects and vice versa. 
Database Tables
        ↕
C# Objects
Q: Benefits of EF Core?
  • Less SQL
  • Faster Development
  • LINQ Support
  • Change Tracking
  • Database Abstraction
Q: Which databases does EF Core support?
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • PostgreSQL
  • MySQL
  • SQLite
Q: Does EF Core generate SQL?
Yes. LINQ queries are automatically translated into SQL statements by EF Core.

49. DbContext

  • DbContext is the primary EF Core class responsible for interacting with the database.
  • It manages database connections, query execution, change tracking, transactions, and saving changes.
  • Think of DbContext as a session between the application and the database.

Real Project Example

public class AppDbContext : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<User> Users { get; set; }

    public DbSet<Order> Orders { get; set; }
}

Registration

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(
    options =>
        options.UseSqlServer(
            connectionString));

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the purpose of DbContext?
DbContext acts as a bridge between the application and the database.
Q: What lifetime should DbContext have?
Scoped lifetime. One instance is created per HTTP request.
Q: Why shouldn't DbContext be Singleton?
  • Not thread-safe
  • Can cause data corruption
  • Can create memory issues
  • Can cause entity tracking problems
Q: What important methods does DbContext provide? 
SaveChanges()

SaveChangesAsync()

Add()

Update()

Remove()

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens when SaveChanges() is called? 
Change Tracking
      ↓
Generate SQL
      ↓
Execute SQL
      ↓
Commit Changes

50. DbSet

  • DbSet represents a database table in EF Core.
  • It provides CRUD operations and querying capabilities for a specific entity type.
  • Each DbSet corresponds to a table in the database.

Real Project Example

Entity

public class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }
}

DbContext

public DbSet<User> Users { get; set; }

Query

var users =
    await _context.Users.ToListAsync();

Follow-up Questions

Q: What does DbSet represent?
A database table.
Q: Can LINQ be used on DbSet? 
_context.Users
        .Where(x => x.IsActive);
Q: Difference between DbSet and DbContext? 
DbContext:
Entire Database Session

DbSet:
Specific Table

51. Change Tracking

  • Change Tracking is the mechanism EF Core uses to monitor entity changes after they are loaded into memory.
  • When SaveChanges() is called, EF Core identifies modified entities and generates appropriate SQL statements.
  • This allows developers to focus on object manipulation rather than SQL updates.

Real Project Example

var user =
    await _context.Users.FindAsync(1);

user.Name = "Ashutosh Updated";

await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
EF Core automatically detects that the Name property changed and generates an UPDATE statement. 
UPDATE Users
SET Name = 'Ashutosh Updated'
WHERE Id = 1

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is Change Tracking useful?
  • Automatically detects Insert operations
  • Automatically detects Update operations
  • Automatically detects Delete operations
Q: What are Entity States? 
Added
Modified
Deleted
Unchanged
Detached
Q: How can you inspect entity state? 
_context.Entry(user).State;

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is the downside of Change Tracking?
For large read-only queries, Change Tracking increases memory and CPU usage. In such scenarios, AsNoTracking() is preferred.

52. Migrations

  • Migrations are used to manage database schema changes through code.
  • They provide version control for database structure changes.
  • Migrations ensure schema updates are applied consistently across environments.

Real Project Example

Suppose a new Email property is added to the User entity. 
public string Email { get; set; }

Create Migration

Add-Migration AddEmailColumn

Generated Migration

migrationBuilder.AddColumn<string>(
    name: "Email",
    table: "Users");

Apply Migration

Update-Database

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Migrations?
  • Version Control
  • Automated Schema Updates
  • Team Collaboration
Q: What command creates a migration? 
Add-Migration MigrationName
Q: What command applies migrations? 
Update-Database
Q: Can migrations be rolled back? 
Update-Database PreviousMigration

53. Code First vs Database First

  • Code First and Database First are two approaches for developing applications with Entity Framework Core.
  • Code First starts with C# classes and generates the database schema from code.
  • Database First starts with an existing database and generates C# entity classes from the database.
  • Code First is generally preferred for new applications, while Database First is useful for legacy databases.

Code First

In the Code First approach, developers create entity classes first and then use migrations to generate and update the database schema. 
C# Classes
      ↓
Migration
      ↓
Database

Example

public class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Database First

In the Database First approach, an existing database is used as the source, and EF Core generates entity classes and DbContext automatically. 
Database
      ↓
Scaffold
      ↓
C# Classes

Example

Scaffold-DbContext

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which approach is more common today?
Code First is more common, especially for new applications because it integrates naturally with migrations and source control.
Q: When is Database First useful?
Database First is useful when working with legacy databases or databases managed by another team.
Q: Which approach supports migrations naturally?
Code First supports migrations naturally because the schema is generated and maintained from code.

54. Eager Loading

  • Eager Loading loads related entities together with the main entity in a single query.
  • It is useful when related data is definitely required.
  • Eager Loading reduces the number of database round trips.
  • EF Core provides the Include() and ThenInclude() methods to perform Eager Loading.

Real Project Example

Suppose an Order entity contains related OrderItems. Instead of loading them separately, both can be retrieved in one query. 
Order
   ↓
OrderItems
var orders =
    await _context.Orders
        .Include(x => x.OrderItems)
        .ToListAsync();
EF Core retrieves both Orders and OrderItems together.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which method enables Eager Loading? 
Include()
Q: Why use Eager Loading?
Eager Loading helps avoid multiple database calls and improves performance when related data is definitely required.
Q: What is ThenInclude?
ThenInclude is used to load deeper relationships from already included entities. 
.Include(o => o.OrderItems)
.ThenInclude(i => i.Product)

55. Lazy Loading

  • Lazy Loading loads related entities only when they are accessed.
  • It can reduce the size of the initial query.
  • Data is fetched automatically when navigation properties are used.
  • While convenient, it may lead to excessive database calls if not used carefully.

Real Project Example

var order =
    await _context.Orders.FirstAsync();

var items =
    order.OrderItems;
When OrderItems is accessed, EF Core automatically loads the related records from the database.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Advantage of Lazy Loading?
Data is loaded only when needed, which can reduce the amount of data retrieved initially.
Q: Disadvantage?
The biggest disadvantage is the N+1 Query Problem, which can significantly affect performance.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is the N+1 Query Problem?
The N+1 Query Problem occurs when one query loads a collection and then additional queries are executed for each related entity. 
foreach(var order in orders)
{
    Console.WriteLine(
        order.Customer.Name);
}
1 Query For Orders
100 Queries For Customers

Total:
101 Queries
This is a major performance issue in enterprise applications and is one reason Eager Loading is often preferred.

56. Explicit Loading

  • Explicit Loading allows developers to manually load related data when required.
  • It provides more control than Lazy Loading.
  • Related entities are loaded only when the developer explicitly requests them.
  • Explicit Loading is useful when related data is needed only in specific scenarios.

Real Project Example

var order =
    await _context.Orders.FirstAsync();
Related data can be loaded later when required. 
await _context.Entry(order)
    .Collection(x => x.OrderItems)
    .LoadAsync();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Explicit Loading?
Explicit Loading is useful when related data is required only under certain conditions and should not always be retrieved.
Q: Difference from Lazy Loading? 
Lazy Loading:
Automatic

Explicit Loading:
Manual

Quick Revision Table

Loading Type Query Count Control
Eager Loading Usually 1 Medium
Lazy Loading Multiple Automatic
Explicit Loading Multiple Full Control

57. AsNoTracking

  • By default, EF Core tracks all entities retrieved from the database so that it can detect changes and generate UPDATE statements during SaveChanges().
  • For read-only operations, change tracking creates unnecessary memory and CPU overhead.
  • AsNoTracking() disables change tracking and improves query performance.
  • It is commonly used in production APIs for dashboards, reports, search results, and lookup data where updates are not required.

Real Project Example

Without AsNoTracking, EF Core tracks every retrieved entity. For read-only scenarios, this tracking is unnecessary.

💻 Without AsNoTracking

var users = await _context.Users
    .ToListAsync();

💻 With AsNoTracking

var users = await _context.Users
    .AsNoTracking()
    .ToListAsync();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use AsNoTracking?
  • Better Performance
  • Lower Memory Usage
  • Faster Queries
Q: When should AsNoTracking be used?
  • Reports
  • Dashboards
  • Search Results
  • Lookup Data
Q: Can tracked entities be updated automatically? 
user.Name = "Updated";

await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
Yes. EF Core automatically detects the modification and generates the appropriate UPDATE statement.
Q: What happens if we modify an AsNoTracking entity?
EF Core will not detect the changes automatically because the entity is not being tracked.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Should AsNoTracking be used everywhere?
No. If the data needs to be updated later in the request lifecycle, change tracking is required. Use AsNoTracking only for read-only operations.

58. Transactions

  • A transaction ensures that multiple database operations are treated as a single unit of work.
  • Either all operations succeed or all operations fail.
  • Transactions help maintain data consistency and prevent partial updates.
  • They are critical when multiple related operations must complete together.

Real Project Example

Consider a bank transfer where money is debited from one account and credited to another. Both operations must succeed together. 
Debit Account A
Credit Account B

💻 Transaction Example

using var transaction =
    await _context.Database
                  .BeginTransactionAsync();

try
{
    accountA.Balance -= 1000;

    accountB.Balance += 1000;

    await _context.SaveChangesAsync();

    await transaction.CommitAsync();
}
catch
{
    await transaction.RollbackAsync();
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use transactions?
To ensure data consistency and prevent partial updates.
Q: What happens if one operation fails?
The entire transaction is rolled back, ensuring the database remains in a consistent state.
Q: What is Commit? 
await transaction.CommitAsync();
Commit permanently saves all transaction changes.
Q: What is Rollback? 
await transaction.RollbackAsync();
Rollback undoes all pending changes within the transaction.
Q: Does SaveChanges automatically use transactions?
Yes. For a single SaveChanges() call, EF Core automatically wraps the operation inside a transaction.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When would you create manual transactions?
When multiple SaveChanges() calls or multiple business operations must succeed together. 
Order Creation
Inventory Update
Payment Update

59. Concurrency Handling

  • Concurrency occurs when multiple users attempt to modify the same record simultaneously.
  • Concurrency handling prevents one user's changes from overwriting another user's updates.
  • EF Core supports optimistic concurrency through concurrency tokens.
  • Optimistic concurrency is the most commonly used approach in enterprise applications.

Real Project Example

Suppose two users open and modify the same employee record simultaneously. 
User A → Update Salary
User B → Update Salary
Without concurrency control: 
Last Save Wins
This can result in data loss.

💻 RowVersion Example

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }

    [Timestamp]
    public byte[] RowVersion { get; set; }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is Optimistic Concurrency?
Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare and validates data before performing updates.
Q: What exception is thrown on conflict? 
DbUpdateConcurrencyException
Q: What is RowVersion?
A SQL Server column that automatically changes whenever a row is updated.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is Optimistic Concurrency preferred?
Because continuously locking rows reduces scalability. Most enterprise systems use optimistic concurrency for better performance and scalability.

60. IQueryable vs IEnumerable (EF Core Perspective)

  • IQueryable and IEnumerable both work with collections but execute queries differently.
  • IQueryable executes on the database side.
  • IEnumerable executes in application memory.
  • For EF Core queries, IQueryable is generally preferred until the final result is required.

Real Project Example

IQueryable

var query =
    _context.Users
            .Where(x => x.IsActive);
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = 1
Filtering occurs directly inside SQL Server.

IEnumerable

var users =
    _context.Users
            .ToList()
            .Where(x => x.IsActive);
Load All Users
        ↓
Filter In Memory
This approach is less efficient for large datasets.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which one executes in SQL Server?
IQueryable.
Q: Which one executes in memory?
IEnumerable.
Q: Which performs better for large datasets?
IQueryable because filtering occurs in the database.
Q: When does IQueryable execute?
IQueryable uses deferred execution. The query runs only when the result is actually requested. 
ToList()

First()

Count()

Any()

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why should IQueryable be used carefully?
Exposing IQueryable outside repositories or services can allow callers to build inefficient queries. Many teams restrict query composition to repository or service layers.

61. Performance Optimization in EF Core

  • Performance optimization in EF Core focuses on reducing database calls, minimizing memory usage, and generating efficient SQL.
  • Most performance issues originate from inefficient query design rather than EF Core itself.
  • Fetching only required data is one of the most effective optimization techniques.

Real Project Example

❌ Bad

var users =
    await _context.Users.ToListAsync();
users.Select(x =>
    new UserDto
    {
        Name = x.Name
    });
This loads all columns from the Users table even if only the Name property is required.

✅ Better

var users =
    await _context.Users
        .Select(x =>
            new UserDto
            {
                Name = x.Name
            })
        .ToListAsync();
Only the required columns are fetched from the database.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Common EF Core optimization techniques?
  • AsNoTracking()
  • Projection
  • Pagination
  • Proper Indexes
  • Avoid N+1 Queries
Q: Why use projection?
Projection fetches only the required columns from the database.
Q: Why avoid SELECT *?
  • Reduces network traffic
  • Lowers memory consumption
  • Improves query execution time

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What are the most common EF Core performance problems?
  • N+1 Queries
  • Missing Indexes
  • Loading Entire Tables
  • Excessive Tracking
  • Multiple Database Round Trips

62. Bulk Operations

  • Bulk operations involve inserting, updating, or deleting large numbers of records efficiently.
  • Standard EF Core operations process entities individually.
  • For large datasets, bulk operations can significantly improve performance.

Real Project Example

❌ Standard Approach

foreach(var user in users)
{
    _context.Users.Add(user);
}

await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
For thousands of records, this approach can become slow.

✅ Better Approach

Bulk Insert
Bulk Update
Bulk Delete
These operations are typically implemented using specialized third-party libraries.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why are bulk operations faster?
  • Reduce SQL Commands
  • Reduce Network Calls
  • Reduce Tracking Overhead
Q: When are bulk operations useful?
  • Data Imports
  • Data Migration
  • Batch Processing

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Does EF Core provide native bulk insert?
Not directly. Most teams use third-party libraries when handling large-scale bulk operations.

63. Repository Pattern with EF Core

  • The Repository Pattern abstracts data access logic behind interfaces.
  • Repositories encapsulate EF Core operations and separate data access from business logic.
  • This improves maintainability, testability, and separation of concerns.

Real Project Example

Repository Interface

public interface IUserRepository
{
    Task<List<User>> GetAllAsync();
}

Repository Implementation

public class UserRepository
    : IUserRepository
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public UserRepository(
        AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public async Task<List<User>> GetAllAsync()
    {
        return await _context.Users
            .ToListAsync();
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Repository Pattern?
  • Separation of Concerns
  • Testability
  • Reusability
Q: Does EF Core already behave like a repository? 
DbSet = Repository
DbContext = Unit Of Work
This is a common discussion point in senior-level interviews.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Should every project use Repository Pattern?
Not necessarily. For simple applications, DbContext may be sufficient. For large enterprise systems, repositories can improve maintainability and architectural consistency.

64. Unit of Work Pattern

  • The Unit of Work Pattern coordinates multiple repository operations into a single transaction.
  • Its primary goal is to ensure related changes are committed together.
  • It helps maintain consistency across multiple repositories and business operations.

Real Project Example

Suppose an order creation process involves multiple related operations. 
Create Order
Update Inventory
Create Payment Record
All operations should succeed together.

Unit Of Work Interface

public interface IUnitOfWork
{
    Task<int> SaveChangesAsync();
}

Implementation

public class UnitOfWork : IUnitOfWork
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public UnitOfWork(
        AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public Task<int> SaveChangesAsync()
    {
        return _context.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What problem does Unit of Work solve?
It coordinates multiple changes into a single commit operation.
Q: Does EF Core already implement Unit of Work? 
DbContext = Unit Of Work
Many developers consider DbContext to be an implementation of the Unit of Work pattern because SaveChanges() commits all tracked changes together.
Q: Why do some teams still create a UnitOfWork class?
  • Abstraction
  • Consistency
  • Easier Testing
  • Architecture Standards

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Repository + UnitOfWork vs Direct DbContext? 
Small Applications
↓
Direct DbContext

Large Enterprise Applications
↓
Repository + UnitOfWork
For small projects, direct DbContext usage is often sufficient. Large enterprise systems may benefit from Repository and Unit of Work patterns for consistency and maintainability.

topics.title: Authentication Authorization
topics.html:
65. Authentication vs Authorization

Security Fundamentals

Authentication and Authorization are two fundamental security concepts used in ASP.NET Core applications. Authentication answers the question "Who are you?", while Authorization answers "What are you allowed to do?".

Interview Answer

  • Authentication verifies user identity.
  • Authorization determines access permissions.
  • Authentication must occur before Authorization.
  • Commonly implemented using JWT, Roles, and Policies.
  • Essential for securing APIs and applications.

Real Project Example

Authentication Flow
Username + Password
       ↓
Authentication
       ↓
JWT Token Issued
Authorization Flow
JWT Token
      ↓
Authorization Check
      ↓
Access Granted/Denied

Follow-up Questions

Can Authorization happen without Authentication?

No. The application must know the user's identity before checking permissions.

Example of Authentication?

Login Screen.

Example of Authorization?

Admin users can delete users while normal users cannot.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Where are Authentication and Authorization implemented?

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

Authentication Middleware must execute before Authorization Middleware.

66. JWT Authentication

Authentication

JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact and secure mechanism for transmitting identity information between a client and server. It enables stateless authentication and is widely used in modern APIs.

Interview Answer

  • JWT is issued after successful login.
  • Client sends JWT with every request.
  • Server validates the token and identifies the user.
  • No server-side session storage is required.
  • Ideal for distributed and microservice architectures.

Real Project Example

Login Request
POST /api/auth/login
Response
{
   "token":"eyJhbGciOi..."
}
Subsequent Requests
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
JWT Configuration
builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(
        JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.TokenValidationParameters =
            new TokenValidationParameters
            {
            };
    });

Follow-up Questions

Why use JWT?

  • Stateless
  • Scalable
  • Secure
  • Cross-platform

Where is JWT stored?

  • HttpOnly Cookie
  • Local Storage
  • Session Storage

What header carries JWT?

Authorization: Bearer Token

Senior-Level Follow-up

JWT is preferred in microservices because every service can independently validate the token without relying on shared session storage.

67. JWT Token Structure

JWT Internals

A JWT consists of three parts separated by dots and is commonly represented as: 

Header.Payload.Signature
xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

JWT Components

Header

{
  "alg":"HS256",
  "typ":"JWT"
}

Payload

{
  "sub":"123",
  "name":"Ashutosh",
  "role":"Admin"
}

Signature

Header
+
Payload
+
Secret Key

Follow-up Questions

Can JWT payload be decoded?

Yes. JWT is encoded, not encrypted.

Should sensitive information be stored in JWT?

No. Anyone possessing the token can decode the payload.

What protects JWT from tampering?

Signature validation.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Although the payload is visible, attackers cannot modify it without invalidating the JWT signature.

68. Refresh Tokens

Token Management

Refresh Tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens after a JWT expires. They improve security by allowing access tokens to remain short-lived.

Real Project Example

Access Token: 15 Minutes

Refresh Token: 7 Days
Access Token Expires
        ↓
Refresh Token Sent
        ↓
New Access Token Generated

Follow-up Questions

Why not create long-lived JWTs?

Because they increase security risk if compromised.

Where should Refresh Tokens be stored?

  • Database
  • HttpOnly Cookie

Can Refresh Tokens be revoked?

Yes. This is one of their biggest advantages.

Senior-Level Follow-up

If a Refresh Token is compromised, it should be revoked immediately and the user should be forced to authenticate again.

69. Claims & Roles

Authorization

Claims contain information about a user, while Roles represent permission groups used for authorization decisions.

Real Project Example

Claims
{
   "UserId":"1",
   "Email":"user@test.com",
   "Role":"Admin"
}
Role-Based Authorization
[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
public IActionResult DeleteUser()
{
    return Ok();
}

Follow-up Questions

What is a Claim?

  • UserId
  • Email
  • Role

What is a Role?

Admin
Manager
User

Where are Claims stored?

Typically inside JWT tokens.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Role  → High-Level Permission

Claim → Any User Information

Claims provide greater flexibility than Roles.

75. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

Interview Answer

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that controls whether a web application can access resources from a different domain, protocol, or port.

By default, browsers block cross-origin requests for security reasons. ASP.NET Core provides built-in CORS Middleware to allow trusted origins to access APIs.

  • Prevents unauthorized cross-domain access
  • Protects browser-based applications
  • Configured using CORS policies
  • Commonly used with React, Angular, and Vue frontends

Real Project Example

React Application: 

http://localhost:3000

ASP.NET Core API: 

https://api.company.com

Browser blocks requests unless CORS is configured.

CORS Configuration

builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("ReactPolicy",
        policy =>
        {
            policy.WithOrigins(
                "http://localhost:3000")
                  .AllowAnyHeader()
                  .AllowAnyMethod();
        });
});

app.UseCors("ReactPolicy");
Follow-up Questions

Q: What problem does CORS solve?

Controls which external websites can access your API.

Q: What causes a CORS error?

Browser blocks requests from unauthorized origins.

Q: Is CORS enforced by the server?

No. CORS is enforced by browsers.

Q: What is an Origin?

Combination of: 

Protocol + Domain + Port
Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why should AllowAnyOrigin() be used carefully?

It allows any website to access the API, which may introduce security risks for sensitive applications.

76. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)

Interview Answer

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is a security attack where a malicious website tricks an authenticated user into performing unintended actions on another website.

The attack works because the browser automatically sends authentication cookies with requests.

  • Targets cookie-based authentication
  • Exploits trusted browser sessions
  • Can trigger unwanted actions
  • Prevented using Anti-Forgery Tokens

Attack Example

User Logged Into Bank
        ↓
Visits Malicious Website
        ↓
Hidden Request Sent
        ↓
Money Transfer Executed
Follow-up Questions

Q: What causes CSRF?

Automatic cookie submission by the browser.

Q: How is CSRF prevented?

Using Anti-Forgery Tokens.

Q: Does JWT Authentication have the same CSRF risk?

Typically less vulnerable when JWT is sent through Authorization headers instead of cookies.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When is CSRF protection most important?

Applications using cookie-based authentication such as MVC applications and web portals.

77. HTTPS & SSL/TLS

Interview Answer

HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is the secure version of HTTP that encrypts communication between clients and servers.

HTTPS uses SSL/TLS certificates to protect data from interception, tampering, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

  • Encrypts transmitted data
  • Verifies server identity
  • Protects sensitive information
  • Required for modern web applications

Request Flow

Browser
   ↓
TLS Handshake
   ↓
Encrypted Connection
   ↓
ASP.NET Core API

ASP.NET Core Configuration

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use HTTPS?

  • Security
  • Data Encryption
  • Identity Verification

Q: What does TLS do?

Encrypts communication between client and server.

Q: Can JWT tokens be sent over HTTP?

Technically yes, but this is insecure and strongly discouraged.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is SSL Termination?

A reverse proxy handles HTTPS encryption while forwarding requests internally to backend services.

78. Data Protection API

Interview Answer

The ASP.NET Core Data Protection API provides secure encryption and decryption capabilities for application data.

It is commonly used for authentication cookies, tokens, and sensitive application data.

Example

public class EncryptionService
{
    private readonly IDataProtector
        _protector;

    public EncryptionService(
        IDataProtectionProvider provider)
    {
        _protector =
            provider.CreateProtector(
                "MyProtector");
    }
}
Follow-up Questions

Q: What is IDataProtector?

A service used to encrypt and decrypt data.

Q: Why use Data Protection API instead of custom encryption?

It provides secure, tested, and framework-supported encryption functionality.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Where are encryption keys stored?

Keys can be stored on the file system, Azure Key Vault, Redis, databases, or other secure providers.

79. Password Hashing

Interview Answer

Password hashing is the process of converting passwords into irreversible hash values before storing them.

Applications should never store plain-text passwords.

  • Protects user credentials
  • Hashes are one-way operations
  • Commonly combined with salts
  • Used by ASP.NET Core Identity

Example Flow

Password
    ↓
Hash Function
    ↓
Stored Hash
Follow-up Questions

Q: Why not encrypt passwords?

Passwords should be hashed because they do not need to be decrypted.

Q: What is a Salt?

Random data added before hashing to prevent rainbow table attacks.

Q: Does ASP.NET Core Identity hash passwords automatically?

Yes.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens if a database is compromised?

Properly hashed passwords are significantly harder to recover than plain-text passwords.

80. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

Interview Answer

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a security vulnerability where attackers inject malicious JavaScript into a web application.

When another user views the compromised page, the malicious script executes in their browser and can steal cookies, tokens, session data, or perform actions on behalf of the user.

Preventing XSS is critical for protecting user accounts and sensitive application data.

  • Client-side security vulnerability
  • Executes malicious JavaScript
  • Can steal cookies and tokens
  • Prevented through validation and encoding

Real Project Example

Vulnerable code: 

<div>
    User Comment
</div>

Attacker submits: 

<script>
alert('Hacked');
</script>

The browser executes the injected script.

Types of XSS
  • Stored XSS
  • Reflected XSS
  • DOM-Based XSS
Follow-up Questions

Q: What is XSS?

Injection of malicious JavaScript into a web application.

Q: What can attackers steal using XSS?

  • Cookies
  • JWT Tokens
  • Session Information
  • User Data

Q: How can XSS be prevented?

  • Input Validation
  • Output Encoding
  • Content Security Policy (CSP)
  • Avoiding Unsafe HTML Rendering
Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why are HttpOnly cookies useful against XSS?

JavaScript cannot directly access HttpOnly cookies, reducing the risk of credential theft.

81. Security Headers

Interview Answer

Security Headers are HTTP response headers that instruct browsers to apply additional security protections.

They help prevent common attacks such as XSS, Clickjacking, MIME-type attacks, and insecure communication.

  • Improve browser security
  • Reduce attack surface
  • Protect against common vulnerabilities
  • Easy to implement globally

Common Security Headers

Header Purpose
Content-Security-Policy Prevents XSS
X-Frame-Options Prevents Clickjacking
X-Content-Type-Options Prevents MIME Sniffing
Strict-Transport-Security Forces HTTPS
Follow-up Questions

Q: What is CSP?

Content Security Policy restricts which scripts and resources browsers are allowed to load.

Q: What is Clickjacking?

A technique where attackers trick users into clicking hidden elements inside an iframe.

Q: What header enforces HTTPS?

Strict-Transport-Security
Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which security header provides the strongest XSS protection?

Content Security Policy (CSP) is one of the most effective browser-level defenses against XSS attacks.

82. Secrets Management

Interview Answer

Secrets Management is the practice of securely storing and accessing sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, connection strings, certificates, and encryption keys.

Hardcoding secrets directly into source code is a major security risk and should always be avoided.

  • Protects sensitive credentials
  • Reduces risk of accidental exposure
  • Supports secure deployments
  • Required for enterprise applications

Bad Example

string password =
    "MySecretPassword";

Better Approach

Environment Variables

Azure Key Vault

User Secrets
Follow-up Questions

Q: What is a secret?

  • API Keys
  • Passwords
  • Connection Strings
  • Certificates

Q: Why avoid storing secrets in source code?

Source code may be shared, committed to repositories, or exposed accidentally.

Q: What is User Secrets?

A development-only feature for storing sensitive values outside source code.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What is the biggest risk of leaked secrets?

Unauthorized access to systems, databases, cloud resources, and customer data.

83. Azure Key Vault

Interview Answer

Azure Key Vault is a cloud service that securely stores and manages secrets, keys, certificates, and cryptographic material.

Instead of storing secrets inside application configuration files, applications retrieve them securely from Key Vault at runtime.

  • Centralized secret storage
  • Secure access control
  • Automatic secret rotation support
  • Enterprise-grade security

It centralizes secret management and provides strong security, auditing, and access control.

84. API Security Best Practices

Interview Answer

API Security Best Practices are techniques used to protect APIs from unauthorized access, data breaches, abuse, and common web attacks.

Secure APIs combine authentication, authorization, encryption, validation, logging, monitoring, and rate limiting.

To prevent abuse, brute-force attacks, and service overload.

Q: Why log security events?

To detect suspicious activity and investigate incidents.

topics.html:
75. SOLID Principles

Interview Answer

SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help create maintainable, scalable, and loosely coupled software.

The Five SOLID Principles:
  • Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
  • Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
  • Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
  • Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
  • Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

In enterprise applications, SOLID principles improve code readability, testability, and long-term maintainability.

Real Project Example

Instead of creating one large service that handles:

Responsibilities
Validation
Database Access
Email Sending
Logging

We separate responsibilities into dedicated classes. This follows SRP and makes the code easier to maintain.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why are SOLID principles important?

  • Loose Coupling
  • Easier Testing
  • Better Maintainability
  • Easier Extension

Q: Which SOLID principle is used most often?

Commonly Used
SRP
DIP

These directly influence everyday coding and architecture decisions.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Does following SOLID guarantee good architecture?

No. SOLID helps improve design but must be applied appropriately. Overengineering can be as harmful as poor design.

76. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

Interview Answer

A class should have only one reason to change. In other words, a class should have only one responsibility.

Bad Example

SRP Violation
public class UserService
{
    public void SaveUser()
    {
    }

    public void SendEmail()
    {
    }

    public void GenerateReport()
    {
    }
}

Multiple responsibilities exist in the same class.

Better Example

User Service
public class UserService
{
    public void SaveUser()
    {
    }
}
Email Service
public class EmailService
{
    public void SendEmail()
    {
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Benefits of SRP?

  • Easier Testing
  • Easier Maintenance
  • Reduced Coupling

Q: How do you identify SRP violations?

Question to Ask
Does this class have multiple reasons to change?

If the answer is yes, SRP is likely being violated.

77. Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

Interview Answer

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

We should be able to add new functionality without changing existing working code.

Bad Example

Hard-Coded Logic
if(paymentType == "CreditCard")
{
}
else if(paymentType == "PayPal")
{
}

Every new payment type requires modifying existing code.

Better Example

Abstraction
public interface IPaymentProcessor
{
    void Process();
}
Implementations
CreditCardProcessor
PayPalProcessor
UPIProcessor

New processors can be added without modifying existing logic.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which pattern commonly supports OCP?

Strategy Pattern.

Q: Why is OCP valuable?

It reduces the risk of breaking existing functionality.

78. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

Interview Answer

Derived classes should be replaceable with their base classes without changing application behavior.

If a subclass cannot properly fulfill the contract of its parent, LSP is violated.

Bad Example

Base Class
public class Bird
{
    public virtual void Fly()
    {
    }
}
LSP Violation
public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly()
    {
        throw new Exception();
    }
}

Penguins cannot fly, therefore the derived class violates the parent contract.

Better Design

Abstraction
IFlyable

Implement only for birds that can actually fly.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is LSP important?

It ensures inheritance remains predictable and reliable.

Q: Common sign of LSP violation?

Warning Sign
NotImplementedException

Frequently throwing exceptions from derived classes is often a sign of an LSP violation.

79. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

Interview Answer

Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.

Large interfaces should be split into smaller, focused interfaces.

Bad Example

Fat Interface
public interface IWorker
{
    void Work();

    void Eat();

    void Sleep();
}

Not all implementations need every method.

Better Example

Work Interface
public interface IWorkable
{
    void Work();
}
Eat Interface
public interface IEatable
{
    void Eat();
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why avoid large interfaces?

They create unnecessary dependencies and force implementations to support unused functionality.

Q: What is another name for ISP?

Fat Interface Prevention Principle.

80. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

Interview Answer

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

This principle is the foundation of Dependency Injection.

Bad Example

Tightly Coupled
public class UserService
{
    private SqlRepository _repo =
        new SqlRepository();
}

Better Example

Dependency Injection
public class UserService
{
    private readonly IUserRepository _repo;

    public UserService(
        IUserRepository repo)
    {
        _repo = repo;
    }
}

Follow-up Questions

Q: How is DIP implemented in ASP.NET Core?

Using Dependency Injection.

Q: Why use abstractions?

Abstractions allow implementations to be replaced without changing consuming classes.

81. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

Interview Answer

CQRS separates read operations from write operations.

Commands modify data, while Queries retrieve data. This separation improves scalability, maintainability, and performance.

Interview Answer

The Factory Pattern creates objects without exposing object creation logic to consumers.

Instead of using new directly, a factory decides which object should be created.

    }

Payment Providers

84. Singleton Pattern

Interview Answer

The Singleton Pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout the application's lifetime.

Example

Singleton Implementation
public class CacheService
{

        _instance =

Interview Answer

The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms and allows them to be swapped at runtime.

Instead of large if-else blocks, behavior is selected dynamically.

Strategies

86. Microservices vs Monolith

Interview Answer

A Monolithic architecture contains all functionality in a single deployable application.

A Microservices architecture breaks functionality into independently deployable services.

Monolith

Architecture
UI
Business Logic
Database

Single deployment unit.

Microservices

Architecture
User Service

Order Service

Each service can be deployed independently.

  • Simpler Development
  • Easier Deployment
  • Easier Debugging

Q: Advantages of Microservices?

  • Independent Scaling
  • Independent Deployment
  • Better Team Ownership

Q: When choose Microservices?

Large systems with multiple teams and significant scaling requirements.

87. Clean Architecture

Interview Answer

Clean Architecture organizes code into layers with dependencies pointing inward toward business rules.

The business layer remains independent of frameworks, databases, and UI technologies.

This approach improves maintainability, testability, and long-term scalability by ensuring that core business logic is not tightly coupled to external systems.

Architecture Layers

Layer Structure
Presentation Layer
        ↓
Application Layer
        ↓
Domain Layer
        ↓
Infrastructure Layer
Dependency Rule:
  • Dependencies always point inward.
  • Outer layers depend on inner layers.
  • Business rules remain isolated from technical concerns.

Responsibilities of Each Layer

Layer Responsibility
Presentation Controllers, APIs, UI Interaction
Application Use Cases, Business Workflows
Domain Core Business Rules & Entities
Infrastructure Database, External Services, File Systems

Real Project Example

Project Flow
API
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Domain
 ↓
Infrastructure
 ↓
SQL Server

Controllers communicate with the Application layer, which executes business rules defined in the Domain layer. Infrastructure handles technical concerns such as databases and third-party integrations.

Benefits

  • High Testability
  • Loose Coupling
  • Technology Independence
  • Better Maintainability
  • Improved Scalability

Follow-up Questions

Q: Main benefit of Clean Architecture?

Business logic becomes independent of external technologies such as databases, frameworks, and UI libraries.

Q: Why is Clean Architecture popular?

  • Testability
  • Maintainability
  • Scalability
  • Technology Independence

Q: Does Clean Architecture increase project complexity?

Yes. It introduces additional layers and abstractions, which may be unnecessary for small applications.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which layer contains business rules?

Answer
Domain Layer

The Domain layer contains the core business entities, rules, and logic that should remain stable regardless of technology changes.

88. Onion Architecture

Interview Answer

Onion Architecture is similar to Clean Architecture and organizes applications into concentric layers around a central Domain layer.

The key principle is that dependencies always point inward toward the core business logic.

The Domain layer sits at the center of the application and remains independent of infrastructure, databases, frameworks, and user interfaces.

Architecture Layers

Onion Layers
Infrastructure
      ↓
Application
      ↓
Domain
Core Concept:
  • Domain layer is at the center.
  • Outer layers depend on inner layers.
  • Business rules remain isolated from implementation details.

Real Project Example

Application Structure
API
 ↓
Services
 ↓
Domain
 ↓
Repositories
 ↓
Database

The API layer communicates with services, which execute business logic in the Domain layer. Repository implementations and databases remain outside the core domain.

Benefits

  • Strong Separation of Concerns
  • High Testability
  • Technology Independence
  • Maintainable Codebase
  • Flexible Infrastructure Changes

Clean Architecture vs Onion Architecture

Aspect Clean Architecture Onion Architecture
Focus Use Cases & Business Rules Domain-Centric Design
Structure Layered Circles Concentric Onion Layers
Dependency Direction Inward Inward
Domain Independence Yes Yes

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between Onion and Clean Architecture?

Both share similar goals:

  • Separation of Concerns
  • Dependency Rule
  • High Testability
  • Maintainable Business Logic

Clean Architecture is generally broader and more commonly referenced in modern .NET projects.

Q: Why keep the Domain Layer independent?

Business rules should survive technology changes without requiring modifications to core application logic.

Example Technology Changes
SQL Server → PostgreSQL

React → Angular

REST API → GraphQL

These changes should impact only outer layers while leaving the Domain layer untouched.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When would you choose Clean Architecture or Onion Architecture?

For medium-to-large enterprise applications where maintainability, testability, and long-term scalability are important. For small CRUD applications, the additional complexity may not provide significant benefits.

89. Caching (In-Memory & Distributed)

Interview Answer

Caching is a technique used to temporarily store frequently accessed data so that future requests can be served faster without repeatedly querying the database or external services.

Benefits of Caching

  • Performance
  • Scalability
  • Response Time
  • Reduced Database Load

In ASP.NET Core, the two most common caching approaches are In-Memory Caching and Distributed Caching.

Real Project Example

Without Cache:

Request
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Response

Every request hits the database.

With Cache:

Request
   ↓
Cache
   ↓
Response

Database is only accessed when the cache expires.

In-Memory Cache Example

builder.Services.AddMemoryCache();

Usage:

public class UserService
{
    private readonly IMemoryCache _cache;

```
public UserService(IMemoryCache cache)
{
    _cache = cache;
}

public async Task<User> GetUser(int id)
{
    if(!_cache.TryGetValue(id, out User user))
    {
        user = await _context.Users.FindAsync(id);

        _cache.Set(id,
                   user,
                   TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
    }

    return user;
}
```

}

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is the benefit of caching?

  • Faster Responses
  • Reduced DB Calls
  • Improved Scalability

Q: Difference between In-Memory and Distributed Cache?

```

In-Memory:

Stored Inside Application Memory

Distributed:

Stored In External Cache Server
```

Server A Cache ≠ Server B Cache

This can cause inconsistent data.

```

103. LINQ (Language Integrated Query)

Interview Answer

LINQ (Language Integrated Query) is a feature in .NET that allows querying and manipulating data using C# syntax. It provides a consistent way to query collections, databases, XML documents, and APIs.

Key Benefits

  • Improved Readability
  • Less Boilerplate Code
  • Type Safety
  • Consistent Query Syntax

In real-world ASP.NET Core applications, LINQ is heavily used with Entity Framework Core for filtering, sorting, grouping, joining, and projecting data.

Real Project Example

Without LINQ

``` List activeUsers = new(); foreach(var user in users) { if(user.IsActive) { activeUsers.Add(user); } }
```

With LINQ

``` var activeUsers = users .Where(x => x.IsActive) .ToList();
```

LINQ makes the code cleaner, shorter, and easier to maintain.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What are the two LINQ syntaxes?

Method Syntax

``` users.Where(x => x.IsActive);
```

Query Syntax

``` from user in users where user.IsActive select user;
```

Q: Which syntax is more common?

Method Syntax is more commonly used in modern .NET applications.

Q: Can LINQ work with databases?

Yes. Entity Framework Core translates LINQ queries into SQL queries that execute on the database server.

```
```

104. Common LINQ Operators

Interview Answer

LINQ provides a rich set of operators for querying and transforming data. These operators help filter, project, sort, group, and aggregate information efficiently.

Most Common Operators

  • Where
  • Select

  • GroupBy
  • Join
  • Any
  • All

Real Project Examples

Where

Used for filtering data.

``` var users = _context.Users .Where(x => x.IsActive);
```

Select

Used for projection.

``` var users = _context.Users .Select(x => new { x.Id, x.Name });
```

OrderBy

Used for sorting.

``` var users = _context.Users .OrderBy(x => x.Name);
```

GroupBy

Used for grouping data.

``` var result = users .GroupBy(x => x.Department);
```

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Select?

Select allows fetching only the required fields instead of entire objects.

Q: Why use GroupBy?

GroupBy is used to aggregate and organize data into categories.

Q: Which operator improves performance significantly?

Select() often improves performance because fewer columns are retrieved from the database.

105. FirstOrDefault vs SingleOrDefault

Interview Answer

Both methods retrieve a single item from a collection, but they behave differently when multiple matching records exist.

FirstOrDefault

  • Returns First Matching Record
  • Returns Null If No Record Exists
``` var user = users .FirstOrDefault(x => x.Id == 1);
```

SingleOrDefault

  • Returns Single Matching Record
  • Returns Null If No Record Exists
  • Throws Exception If Multiple Records Exist
``` var user = users .SingleOrDefault(x => x.Email == email);
```

Follow-up Questions

Q: When should SingleOrDefault be used?

Use it when business rules guarantee uniqueness.

  • Email Address
  • Employee Number

Q: Which is safer?

``` FirstOrDefault
```

Because it does not throw an exception if duplicate records exist.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which generates better SQL?

Both generally generate similar SQL. Choose based on business requirements rather than performance.

```
```

106. Deferred Execution

Interview Answer

Deferred Execution means a LINQ query is not executed when it is defined. Instead, execution occurs only when the results are actually needed.

Real Project Example

``` var query = _context.Users .Where(x => x.IsActive);
```
``` No SQL Executed
```

SQL executes only when the query is materialized.

``` var users = await query.ToListAsync();
```

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which methods trigger execution?

``` ToList() First() Count() Any() Single()
```

Q: Benefits of Deferred Execution?

  • Better Performance
  • Flexible Query Building

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is Deferred Execution important in EF Core?

EF Core generates the final SQL query only after all filters, projections, and conditions have been applied.

```
```

113. Parallel Programming (TPL)

Threading & Performance

TPL (Task Parallel Library) enables parallel execution of CPU-intensive operations. Parallel programming differs from asynchronous programming.

Key Concept

  • Async improves scalability.
  • Parallelism improves execution speed.
  • TPL helps utilize multiple CPU cores efficiently.
  • Useful for CPU-bound workloads.

Real Project Example

Parallel.ForEach
Parallel.ForEach(
    users,
    user =>
    {
        ProcessUser(user);
    });

In this example, multiple users can be processed simultaneously across available CPU cores, significantly reducing total execution time.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Async vs Parallel?

Async Programming

I/O Bound Work

Used for operations waiting on external resources such as databases, APIs, or file systems.

Parallel Programming

CPU Bound Work

Used when computations can run simultaneously on multiple CPU cores.

Q: Examples of CPU-bound tasks?

Common CPU-Intensive Operations

  • Image Processing
  • Report Generation
  • Mathematical Calculations
  • Data Compression
  • Video Encoding
  • Large Data Transformations

Interview Tip

A common interview question is the difference between asynchronous programming and parallel programming. Remember: 

Async = Better Scalability

Parallel = Faster CPU Processing

114. Dependency Injection (DI)

ASP.NET Core Fundamentals

Interview Answer

Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern used to achieve loose coupling between classes. Instead of a class creating its own dependencies, the dependencies are provided from outside, usually through the constructor.

ASP.NET Core includes a built-in Dependency Injection container that automatically manages object creation and service lifetimes.

In real-world projects, Dependency Injection is commonly used for services, repositories, logging, caching, and third-party integrations because it improves maintainability, testability, and flexibility.

Benefits of Dependency Injection

  • Loose Coupling
  • Better Testability
  • Easier Maintenance
  • Improved Flexibility

Real Project Example

Without Dependency Injection

Tightly Coupled Service
public class UserService
{
    private readonly UserRepository _repo;

    public UserService()
    {
        _repo = new UserRepository();
    }
}

Problem

Tightly Coupled
Hard To Test

With Dependency Injection

Constructor Injection
public class UserService
{
    private readonly IUserRepository _repo;

    public UserService(IUserRepository repo)
    {
        _repo = repo;
    }
}
Service Registration
builder.Services.AddScoped<
    IUserRepository,
    UserRepository>();

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Dependency Injection?

Benefits

  • Loose Coupling
  • Better Testability
  • Easier Maintenance
  • Better Flexibility

Q: What types of Injection exist?

Injection Types

  • Constructor Injection
  • Property Injection
  • Method Injection
Constructor Injection

Constructor Injection is the most commonly used approach in ASP.NET Core applications.

Q: Why is Constructor Injection preferred?

Because dependencies become explicit and mandatory, making the class easier to understand, maintain, and test.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What problem does DI solve?

Without DI

Class Creates Dependencies

With DI

Container Creates Dependencies

This separation significantly improves maintainability, flexibility, and unit testing.

115. Service Lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton)

Dependency Injection

Interview Answer

ASP.NET Core provides three service lifetimes that determine how long an object remains alive. Choosing the correct lifetime is important for performance, memory management, and thread safety.

Transient

A new instance is created every time the service is requested.

Registration
builder.Services.AddTransient<
    IEmailService,
    EmailService>();
Request Service
      ↓
New Object

Every injection receives a completely new instance.

Scoped

One instance is created per HTTP request.

Registration
builder.Services.AddScoped<
    IUserService,
    UserService>();
Request Starts
      ↓
Same Instance Reused
      ↓
Request Ends

Singleton

A single instance is shared for the entire application lifetime.

Registration
builder.Services.AddSingleton<
    ICacheService,
    CacheService>();
Application Starts
       ↓
One Instance Created
       ↓
Shared Everywhere

Quick Comparison

Lifetime Instance Creation Typical Usage
Transient Every Request For Service Lightweight Services
Scoped Per HTTP Request DbContext, Business Services
Singleton Entire Application Lifetime Cache & Configuration

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which lifetime is used by DbContext?

Scoped

Q: Why shouldn't DbContext be Singleton?

Because DbContext is not thread-safe and sharing a single instance across requests can lead to concurrency and tracking issues.

Q: Common Singleton examples?

Examples

  • Cache Services
  • Configuration Services

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Can Singleton depend on Scoped Service?

No. This causes a runtime exception because a longer-lived service cannot safely consume a shorter-lived service. 

Cannot Consume Scoped Service
From Singleton

116. Middleware

ASP.NET Core Request Pipeline

Interview Answer

Middleware is software that sits in the HTTP request pipeline and processes requests and responses.

Middleware Responsibilities

  • Execute logic before the next middleware
  • Call the next middleware
  • Execute logic after the next middleware

ASP.NET Core applications are built around middleware components that collectively handle every incoming request.

Real Project Example

Request
   ↓
Exception Middleware
   ↓
Authentication Middleware
   ↓
Authorization Middleware
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Response

Custom Middleware

LoggingMiddleware.cs
public class LoggingMiddleware
{
    private readonly RequestDelegate _next;

    public LoggingMiddleware(
        RequestDelegate next)
    {
        _next = next;
    }

    public async Task Invoke(
        HttpContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Request Started");

        await _next(context);

        Console.WriteLine("Request Completed");
    }
}
Registration
app.UseMiddleware<
    LoggingMiddleware>();

117. Middleware Execution Order

ASP.NET Core Request Pipeline

Interview Answer

Middleware order is critical because requests flow through middleware in the order they are registered, while responses flow back in reverse order.

Incorrect middleware ordering can cause authentication failures, authorization issues, security vulnerabilities, and unexpected application behavior.

Important Rule

  • Request travels top to bottom.
  • Response travels bottom to top.
  • Middleware order directly impacts application behavior.

Correct Middleware Order

Program.cs
app.UseExceptionHandler();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Request Flow

Request
   ↓
Exception Handler
   ↓
HTTPS Redirection
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Response

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why must Authentication come before Authorization?

Authorization requires an authenticated user identity before permissions can be evaluated.

Q: What happens if order is incorrect?

Possible Issues

  • Authentication Failures
  • Authorization Failures
  • Security Vulnerabilities
  • Unexpected Runtime Behavior

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: How do requests and responses move through middleware?

Request → Forward

Response ← Reverse

118. Logging (ILogger)

Monitoring & Diagnostics

Interview Answer

Logging is the process of recording application events, warnings, errors, and diagnostic information.

Logging is essential for monitoring, troubleshooting, debugging, and production support.

ASP.NET Core provides ILogger as the built-in logging abstraction.

Why Logging Matters

Using ILogger

Error logging should be used for unexpected failures, exceptions, and operations that cannot be completed successfully.

Q: When use Information logging?

Information logging should be used for normal business operations and important application events.

Q: Why avoid excessive logging?

Excessive logging can increase storage costs, reduce performance, and make important logs difficult to identify.

119. Serilog

Structured Logging

Serilog is a structured logging framework commonly used in ASP.NET Core applications.

Application Settings

Configuration provides a centralized way to store application settings and environment-specific values.

123. Correlation ID

ASP.NET Core - Monitoring & Diagnostics

A Correlation ID is a unique identifier attached to a request that allows tracking the request across multiple services and logs. It is extremely useful in distributed systems and microservices.

Interview Answer

  • Unique identifier assigned to each request.
  • Helps trace requests across services and logs.
  • Improves debugging and monitoring.
  • Commonly used in microservices architectures.
  • Allows end-to-end request tracking.

Real Project Example

A request enters the system and receives a Correlation ID that travels with it through all services. 

Request
  ↓
Correlation ID:
ABC123

Every log entry contains the same identifier.

ABC123 - Database Query

ABC123 - Response Sent

To trace requests across systems.

Q: Where are Correlation IDs stored?

Typically in a request header.

X-Correlation-ID

Q: Why are Correlation IDs critical in Microservices?

Because a single request may travel through multiple services, databases, queues, and APIs. Correlation IDs make it possible to trace the complete request journey across the entire distributed system.

124. API Security Best Practices

Security

API Security is the practice of protecting APIs from unauthorized access, attacks, and data breaches. A secure API ensures that only authorized users can access resources while protecting sensitive data and preventing malicious activity.

Key Security Objectives

  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Data Protection
  • Input Validation
  • Secure Communication

In production applications, security is typically implemented using JWT Authentication, Role/Policy-Based Authorization, HTTPS, Input Validation, Rate Limiting, and secure secret management.

Typical secure API request flow:

Secure API Flow
Client
  ↓
JWT Authentication
  ↓
Authorization

Input Validation
  ↓
Business Logic
  ↓
Database

Q: What are the most important API security measures?

  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • HTTPS
  • Input Validation
  • Rate Limiting

Q: Should APIs expose internal exception details?

No. APIs should return user-friendly error messages while detailed exception information should be logged internally for troubleshooting.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: How do you secure APIs in production?

  • JWT Authentication
  • Role-Based Authorization
